First, multi-agent collaboration does not consistently improve final-answer accuracy over strong single LLMs. Second, collaboration can substantially enhance the coverage of intermediate reasoning, but such gains may come at the cost of increased reasoning redundancy. Third, current systems remain vulnerable to adversarial reasoning errors, particularly those involving subtle structural perturbations. The dataset is available at https://github.com/mira-ai-lab/AgentMath.

Title: Auditable and Deployable Multi-Agent Motion Planning via Posetal Games from Legal Guidelines
Authors: Florian Lercher, Karan Mahesh, Yujun Huang, Meshal Alharbi, Runyu Zhang, Hanna Krasowski, Michael R. Benjamin, Matthias Althoff, Gioele Zardini
Subjects: Multiagent Systems (cs.MA); Computer Science and Game Theory (cs.GT); Robotics (cs.RO); Systems and Control (eess.SY)
Abstract: When robots are deployed in the real-world, they must interact with other agents and accomplish their own goals while adhering to legal constraints. These potentially conflicting objectives are often only partially prioritized, making scalarized objectives or fully specified hierarchies unsuitable. We present a framework for multi-agent motion planning under legal requirements based on games with partially ordered preferences (posetal games). Scenario-independent legal guidelines order abstract legal concerns, from which we automatically derive agent preferences and a legal game for any concrete scenario. Agents may refine their legal preferences with private objectives, and regulators may refine the guideline as laws evolve. We prove that such customizations can only remove equilibria and thus preserve legality. To coordinate agents without explicitly communicating private preferences, we introduce belief play, which provably recovers the true equilibria from conservative local games, and a distributed iterative best-response protocol requiring less information. We apply the framework to maritime navigation, systematically lifting pairwise traffic rules to multi-vessel encounters. On seven encounters with up to four vessels, every rule violation of the committed equilibria is certified as forced by the legal hierarchy or unsatisfiable, and defectors are identified from public information in all tested cases. These results indicate that guideline-based posetal games offer an auditable route from partially specified laws to multi-agent motion planning.

Title: SCARCE: Emergent Institutions in Long-Horizon Multi-Agent Coding Systems
Authors: Abhinav Kumar, Rediet Abebe, Eugene Bagdasarian, Sahar Abdelnabi
Abstract: As autonomous agents become widely deployed, coordinating access to shared computing resources and services will become increasingly important. Recent incidents have already revealed unplanned coordination between agents, highlighting the safety implications of these interactions. Yet prior studies of agent negotiation often use stylized games and simulated bargaining, leaving open how these behaviors develop during sustained, long-horizon tasks. We propose SCARCE (Shared Compute ARena for Coding agEnts), a framework in which agents solve sequences of coding tasks under individual deadlines while negotiating access to a shared execution resource. This negotiation determines when and for how long they can inspect programs, compile code, and run tests. We find that agents spontaneously develop informal institutions: persistent rules and commitments grounded in reputation, reciprocity, and precedent. These arrangements, which we call institutional behaviors, carry across tasks and influence resource allocation, with agents sometimes forgoing immediate advantages to honor earlier agreements. We develop a 21-category taxonomy of negotiation strategies and emergent norms and use it to analyze eight models and audit more than 1,500 trajectories across different environmental settings. Among the models tested, newer frontier models exhibit more institutional behaviors than older or lightweight models. Alongside cooperation, we observe exclusionary coalitions and rare divide-and-conquer strategies. SCARCE provides a controlled setting for proactively and systematically auditing how these relationships emerge, shape access to resources, and affect the safety and coordination of multi-agent systems.

Title: Agentic Cognitive Depth: Operational Criteria for Evaluating LLM Agents
Authors: Nijesh Upreti, Chris Sypherd, Vaishak Belle
Abstract: Agentic large language model (LLM) systems are commonly implemented as an LLM in a loop with Planning, Memory, Tools, and Control Flow. This application-focused view connects agentic LLM research with deployable systems and leaves open how such systems should be evaluated beyond end-to-end task success. Building on this view, we define agentic cognitive depth as a trajectory-level profile across five operational criteria. The profile contains context sensitivity ($C$), temporal continuity ($T$), multimodal coordination ($M$), adaptive interaction ($A$), and metacognitive monitoring ($Mc$). The first four criteria measure how well Control Flow, Memory, Tools, and Planning are used across a trajectory. The fifth measures whether the system monitors and regulates the full run. For each criterion, we give operational proxies and a perturbation procedure, then connect the profile to the agent's world model. We provide the structure needed to extend benchmarks such as GAIA, SWE-bench, WebArena, and TRIP-Bench with per-criterion diagnostics. Symbolic verifiers, structured memory, planner coupling, and tool constraints provide practical ways to build and test these capacities.

Title: Do Rollups Self-Organize? Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning in the EIP-4844 Blob Fee Market
Authors: Alessio Brini
Subjects: Multiagent Systems (cs.MA); Computer Science and Game Theory (cs.GT); Trading and Market Microstructure (q-fin.TR)
Abstract: EIP-4844 gave Ethereum rollups a separate fee dimension for data, governed by a multiplicative update rule that targets three ``blobs''per block. Whether this target is reached depends on how many independent, self-interested rollups choose to post data, a question that closed-form models address only for a single agent under exogenous prices or in a static equilibrium. We propose a calibrated multi-agent reinforcement learning environment for the blob fee market in which the blob base fee is endogenous, set by the EIP-4844 rule on the aggregated decisions of heterogeneous rollups fit to post-Dencun Ethereum data. After confirming that the environment reproduces the known single-agent analytical optimum, we show that independent learners, with no convergence guarantee, still settle near the target without coordination ($3.32\pm0.01$ blobs per block over five seeds). Over a fiftyfold demand range ($10\times$ to $500\times$), supply stays at the target from $10\times$ to $200\times$ and rises above it at higher demand, where the fee can no longer hold it. Posting frequency increases with rollup size, an emergent analog of the size threshold predicted by prior theory. A costless layer-1 calldata outside option pushes the fee down by roughly an order of magnitude while aggregate supply stays at the target, so the fee rule acts as a negative-feedback controller on decentralized supply.

Title: Exact Cut Complexity of Equal-Length Proportional Cake Cutting
Authors: Yasushi Kawase, Bodhayan Roy, Mohammad Azharuddin Sanpui
Subjects: Multiagent Systems (cs.MA); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Data Structures and Algorithms (cs.DS); Computer Science and Game Theory (cs.GT)
Abstract: We study proportional cake cutting under an equal-length constraint, where each of $n$ agents must receive a bundle of length exactly $1/n$ that is worth at least $1/n$ to that agent. Our main result determines the exact worst-case number of cuts needed to guarantee such an allocation, namely $2n-2$ for every $n$. This improves on the previously known quadratic upper bound. The proof combines the constrained necklace-splitting theorem with a recursive assignment argument based on Hall's theorem. The same bound extends to the stronger requirement of envy-freeness when $n$ is a prime power, and an $O(n^{1.525})$ upper bound holds for arbitrary $n$. We then ask whether such allocations can be computed. We first show that no deterministic protocol in the Robertson--Webb model terminates after finitely many queries on every instance and always returns an exact equal-length proportional allocation, even for two agents with identical valuations. For every $\varepsilon>0$, however, $O(n^2/\varepsilon)$ queries suffice to produce an allocation in which every agent receives a bundle of length exactly $1/n$ and value at least $1/n-\varepsilon$, again using at most $2n-2$ cuts. Finally, we augment the Robertson--Webb model with two-knife queries. We show that recursive balanced halving attains the optimal bound of $2n-2$ cuts when $n$ is a power of two. For arbitrary $n$, we give a procedure using $O(n\log n)$ cuts.
Venue: Int Symp Math Found Comput Sci, MFCS, Math Found Comput Sci, Mathematical Foundations of Computer Science

Title: When Agents Collude: Weak-to-Strong On-Policy Distillation for Mitigating Strategic Deception in Multi-Agent Systems
Authors: Eric Onyame, Runtao Zhou, Kowshik Thopalli, Bhavya Kailkhura, Chirag Agarwal
Subjects: Multiagent Systems (cs.MA); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computation and Language (cs.CL); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
Abstract: While recent advances in autonomous agents enable them to coordinate on increasingly complex tasks, prior work shows that this growing capacity for coordination can create safety risks, including collusion, in which agents jointly pursue misaligned actions while concealing the true basis of those actions from oversight. We study this risk in a simulated insider-trading environment, comparing single agents with sequential and decentralized teams across seven language models from three families. By varying agents'system-level objectives and pressure conditions, we examine when coordinated agents act on material nonpublic information, conceal the basis of a misaligned trade in a report, and maintain that deception under follow-up questioning. Compared to single-agent decision-making, multi-agent interaction raises misaligned-action rates from 35.4% to 68.2% and persistent-deception rates from 31.0% to 62.2%, both measured over all runs. These effects are largest under existential pressure, where teams sustain deception through follow-up questioning in 87% of all runs. Qualitative analysis reveals shared cover stories and coordinated rationales, suggesting group-level strategic deception rather than isolated reporting errors. To mitigate this behavior, we introduce PACT, a weak-to-strong on-policy distillation framework for mitigating collusive deception. Using generic honesty prompts, PACT trains a stronger student on its own sampled continuations, matching its next-token distribution to that of a smaller, frozen honesty-aligned teacher via reverse-KL supervision. Under existential pressure with ethical instructions, PACT reduces multi-agent persistent deception from 80% to 3%. Our results show that multi-agent coordination amplifies strategic deception and that on-policy honesty alignment can substantially mitigate these failures.

Title: BE-CTDE: Blockchain-Enabled Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning with Anomaly Detection and Token Economics
Authors: Chih-Wei Huang, Hsin-Chieh Lee, Yun-Chen Yu, Ibrahim Althamary, Rongxing Lu, Phone Lin
Subjects: Multiagent Systems (cs.MA); Cryptography and Security (cs.CR); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Networking and Internet Architecture (cs.NI)
Abstract: Multi-agent reinforcement learning supports cooperative decision-making in Internet of Things systems, but strategic deviations can disrupt coordination and undermine confidence in the training process. This paper proposes Blockchain-Enabled Centralized Training and Decentralized Execution (BE-CTDE), which uses blockchain as an active training-management layer. A behavioral verifier compares executed trajectories with shared-policy recommendations; its flags drive a token mechanism combining slashing, burning, rewards, and compensation. Retained balances determine each agent's contribution to the global policy update, connecting auditable behavior to learning influence. We derive a one-round incentive condition that accounts for action-dependent compensation and the payoff from deviation, and a finite expected exclusion-time bound under explicit conditional detection and accounting assumptions, showing perfect detection is unnecessary. An exact finite-population capacity bound characterizes the limits of the population-relative detector. In multi-agent path finding experiments, BE-CTDE outperforms a state-of-the-art learning-based path planner with substantially higher success rates under attack, even when adversaries form the majority. It also outperforms partially defended baselines in all configurations, with collision rates up to 35% lower than under detection without economic consequences and up to 43% lower than under conventional stake slashing. Together, these results characterize how behavioral verification and token feedback can support accountable cooperative learning.

Title: Pay for the Fault, Not the Flow: Label-Free In-Flow Multi-Agent Workflow Optimization
Authors: Xuehang Guo, Haoyu Wang, Shengyu Chen, Zach Chen, Wei Cheng, Qingyun Wang, Haifeng Chen
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly construct multi-agent workflows that decompose a complex task and assign specialist agents from a pool. However, building such a workflow well remains challenging: how finely to divide the task, which agent to trust with each subtask, and when to create a new specialist are all critical decisions a workflow constructor needs to settle up front. Thus, whether each subtask succeeds remains unknown until the workflow runs. Yet, improving a workflow is costly. Locating a fault usually requires a reference answer, a graded outcome, or a trained assessor, and the fix is applied to the whole workflow through re-execution, re-search, or retraining. We propose InFlowOp, which prices every decision in one label-free cost that weighs how well an agent's competence meets what a subtask demands against how much that agent takes to run. Before execution, InFlowOp bidirectionally determines the granularity of task decomposition and agent assignment following from the cost rather than from a fixed template. During execution, InFlowOp corrects a fault with the cheapest move via the same cost that serves the workflow both as it is built and as it runs. Facing the workflow-level evaluation challenge, we introduce Braid, a benchmark whose tasks require multi-agent coordination beyond single-agent capability. Across various domains and backbones, InFlowOp outperforms single agent baselines by up to $+11.97\%$, achieving $+9.64\%$ with in-flow optimization. Our project page: https://xhguo7.github.io/InFlowOp/.

Title: AECG: Asymmetric Experience Consolidation and Governance In Multi-Agent Systems
Authors: Ao Tian, Jialong Liu, Daqi Zheng, Xin Sun, Mengting Li, Zhizhao Xiao, Zijian Huang, Honglei Wang, Zijian Hei, Yukun Yan
Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems increasingly rely on memory to transform execution trajectories into reusable procedural knowledge. Yet repeated retrieval also makes memory errors persistent: memory pollution arises when outdated, weakly supported, or spuriously successful procedures become recurring components of future reasoning. Multi-agent execution introduces an additional structural risk. Scope collapse occurs when procedural knowledge escapes the coordination scope in which it was shown effective and is repeatedly reused at incompatible decision levels, allowing local errors to influence cascades of downstream decisions. Meanwhile, task-level failures provide ambiguous supervision because they rarely reveal which recalled knowledge was responsible. We introduce AECG, a framework for asymmetric experience consolidation and governance for multi-agent systems. AECG turns memory from static experience storage into a dynamic reliability-governance loop, preserving coordination scope and using multi-scale, confidence-aware reliability to detect degradation. It then combines degradation with downstream impact to prioritize high-risk knowledge under a bounded review budget, applies targeted interventions, and reactivates revised skills only after paired replay. Across three multi-agent frameworks and four benchmarks, AECG achieves the best score in 11 of 12 framework--benchmark settings and improves over the strongest competing memory method by as much as 10.23 percentage points; removing scope preservation reduces accuracy by up to 16.89 points. AECG thereby reframes multi-agent memory from passive accumulation into auditable reliability governance. Code is available at https://github.com/fenhg297/AECG

Title: OOPMAS: Object-Oriented Multi-Agent Systems for Query-Level Workflow Generation
Authors: Qi Cheng, Shengyu Chen, Wei Cheng, Yiqun Xie, Xiaowei Jia, Haoyu Wang, Haifeng Chen
Abstract: Multi-agent systems (MAS) powered by large language models have shown strong performance across code generation, mathematical reasoning, and question answering. However, existing methods for automating MAS design mostly operate at the task level, producing a single fixed workflow per benchmark that is applied uniformly to all queries. This assumption fails under realistic conditions. Query difficulty varies widely within a task, and real-world workloads mix heterogeneous task types. We introduce OOPMAS, a training-free framework that generates both the agent set and the coordination workflow at the granularity of individual queries. Agents are represented as object-oriented class definitions with dedicated roles, tools, and persistent state, and workflows are expressed as executable main functions over these agent objects. A dynamic skill library accumulates structured lessons from execution feedback across optimization rounds, enabling in-context improvement without any gradient updates or fine-tuning. On a mixed-task benchmark of queries spanning code, math, and QA, OOPMAS achieves 89.6% accuracy, outperforming the strongest baseline by 18.1 percentage points. A model-swap study across four LLM backbones shows consistent scaling, reaching 92.4% with the strongest model.

Title: Observe, Share, or Predict? Disentangling Partner Information in Embodied Multi-Agent Collaboration
Authors: Adrián Szlatincsán, Filippo Ziliotto, Bruno Lepri, Luciano Serafini, Massimiliano Luca, Tommaso Campari
Abstract: LLMs are used as high-level controllers for embodied agents, but it remains unclear whether they support collaborative reasoning, such as anticipating a collaborator's actions in real-time teamwork without dialogue. We ask if observing the partner's state, exchanging object knowledge, and predicting the partner's next action, shape task outcomes and coordination when agents can share percepts but never intentions, plans, or task-level messages, and whether the two agents occupy symmetric roles. Using the Habitat-based PARTNR benchmark, we introduce a Decoupled Partial Observability regime that enforces strictly individual perception, and we augment decentralized zero-shot ReAct planners with Other Agent's State (OAS) observation, object Knowledge Exchange (KE) between co-located agents, and Other Agent's Next Action (OANA) prediction, evaluated on the full 2 x 2 x 2 grid with four planners on 1,000 validation tasks. OAS observation improves task quality, reducing extraneous effort for every planner, whereas KE primarily improves execution efficiency, cutting simulation steps by up to 25% with little change in success. The two are largely redundant for strong planners but complementary for the weakest, for which KE without the OAS is the worst configuration. OANA prediction lowers the success rate in 15 of 16 model x context pairs while raising explicit partner mentions to 55-100%, and its accuracy gains lie mainly in the coarse action type, partly because agents recognize the action the partner is already performing. The robot retrieves objects sooner and completes its tasks earlier than the simulated human. Shared context reduces total task time by shortening the remaining duration that the human works alone. Also, coordination benefits arise from responding to shared context, especially the OAS, rather than explicit anticipation, yielding shallow, planner-dependent partner modeling.

Title: MADDIE: Multi-Agent Drug Discovery Engine
Authors: Ye Liu, Reza Averly, Avery Meyer, Frazier N. Baker, Ruoxi Gao, Daniel Adu-Ampratwum, Xia Ning
Abstract: Drug discovery remains a resource-intensive and time-consuming process, involving billions of dollars and a decade of development to advance a drug to market. While many in silico tools have accelerated this process, operating them still demands substantial time, effort, and expertise from medicinal chemists. Autonomous systems built on Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as a promising solution, yet current designs limit their performance. Existing single-agent systems scale poorly to long-horizon, multi-step, and realistic tasks, whereas multi-agent systems typically execute predefined workflows that cannot capture the iterative, non-linear nature of a real drug discovery campaign. Here, we present MADDIE, a multi-agent drug discovery engine. It comprises a central agent, Orchestrator, and four specialized worker agents: HitIdentifier, LeadOptimizer, Synthesizer, and Evaluator, each representing a critical step in a drug discovery campaign. Under Orchestrator's orchestration and coordination, these worker agents are composed into flexible workflows, enabling MADDIE to adapt its strategy and navigate the drug discovery pipeline end-to-end. Across 50 protein targets, MADDIE produces molecules satisfying key property requirements and their synthesis routes, outperforming existing agentic systems, generative models, and general-purpose LLMs by a wide margin. Our analysis reveals how these agents collaborate and that MADDIE can employ different strategies across targets to achieve the campaign's goal, while still being efficient in time and tokens. Together, they demonstrate MADDIE as a low-cost, effective, and efficient autonomous engine for accelerating drug discovery. Code and dataset is available via https://github.com/ninglab/MADDIE.

Title: Learning Adaptive Deliberation Control for Reliable Recognition with Multi-Agent Language Models
Authors: Yuan Liu, Haoyue Peng, Fanliang Hu, Lei Huang, Wenli Cai
Abstract: Multi-agent deliberation can improve recognition by criticizing and revising candidate answers, but fixed controls cannot respond to changes in disagreement or reasoning quality. We present an adaptive multi-agent controller (ADMA) that learns continuous policies for proposal, challenge, arbitration, and coordination while keeping the task model frozen. Shared trace features describe quality, agreement, and progress, while role-specific features support decentralized control during inference. One controller trained on legal and financial reasoning is transferred without policy updates to four textual and multimodal benchmarks and two successive task-model versions. With Qwen3.5 held fixed, ADMA-Full improves accuracy by 6.2-14.2 percentage points over Direct and by 2.8-3.0 points over ADMA-Fixed. Paired bootstrap ranges for the Full-Fixed comparison are positive on three tasks. Outcome decompositions show that recoveries exceed introduced errors, while process assessment records fewer false-consensus events and more supported correct outcomes. Transfer to Qwen3.6 remains task dependent, which bounds the generality of the learned policy. Median token and latency ratios are 14.3-18.7 and 7.8-16.5 relative to Direct. These results show that adaptive deliberation can improve fixed-model recognition when its task-dependent gains justify the additional computation.

Title: Train Locally, Learn Together: Distributed Multi-Agent Training via ADMM
Authors: Yiwei Chen, Changsheng Wang, Yicheng Lang, Qing Qu, Alfred O. Hero, Sijia Liu
Abstract: Multi-agent systems (MAS) can outperform individual language-model agents by combining specialized roles, diverse reasoning processes, and collaborative decision-making. However, collaborative MAS training is typically centralized, requiring a common trainer to aggregate role-local trajectories and learning signals and maintain model and optimization states. This motivates a distributed multi-agent learning paradigm in which agents improve system-level capabilities through role-local learning and decentralized communication, paving the way toward scalable, resilient, and self-organizing MAS. To this end, we introduce, to the best of our knowledge, the first optimization-grounded framework for distributed MAS training based on consensus alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM). We formulate collaborative MAS learning as a consensus-constrained finite-sum optimization problem, naturally lending itself to distributed optimization via ADMM. The proposed approach alternates role-local learning with inter-agent consensus using distributed communication protocols such as ring all-reduce, enabling joint optimization while keeping each agent's data and training state local. We evaluate our framework on distributed safety alignment and general reasoning tasks. Under compromised-agent settings, ADMM can reduce HarmBench attack success rate (ASR) by up to 26.4%, while achieving reasoning gains comparable to centralized training. These results show that distributed MAS training retains the benefits of centralized joint optimization without requiring a centralized trainer.

Title: Beyond Final Accuracy: Auditing Communication in LLM Multi-Agent Systems
Authors: Shixuan Li, Wei Yang, Peiyu Zhang, Anzhe Cheng, Heng Ping, Paul Bogdan
Abstract: Multi-agent communication aims to help agents benefit from one another's information. Yet improvements in system performance leave a fundamental ambiguity: do they reflect effective communication, a favorable agent architecture, or simply additional reasoning? Because communication methods are commonly evaluated within the systems they were designed for, these factors are difficult to disentangle. Final accuracy further merges corrected errors and corrupted answers into a single outcome, obscuring how communication changes decisions. We introduce Independent--Communicate--Revise (ICR), a controlled framework that evaluates communication as answer revision following independent reasoning. ICR fixes initial reasoning trajectories, measures correction and preservation conditional on both agents'initial correctness, and uses a no-message revision control to quantify gains beyond additional reasoning. Across four reasoning benchmarks, our audit of textual and latent communication reveals that similar aggregate accuracy can conceal substantially different revision behaviors. Compared with transmitting answers alone, full reasoning increases correction while reducing preservation on all four benchmarks, so richer messages amplify beneficial and harmful influence alike. Receiver-policy comparisons on MedQA and GPQA-D further show that a structured verification policy shifts every channel toward greater preservation and lower correction, while its effect on selectivity varies across channels and tasks. These findings challenge treating communication quality as an intrinsic property of a channel. ICR therefore recenters evaluation on selective revision, providing a unified framework for examining how message content and receiver policies jointly produce benefits and harms.

Title: Balancing Mobility Efficiency and Environmental Exposure During Mega Events: A Multi-agent Routing Framework
Authors: Xinyue Liu, Qiumeng Li, Suhong Zhou, Junwen Lu, Jiali Zhou, Weipan Xu
Abstract: Mega events can generate concentrated travel demand, intensifying congestion around venues and increasing travelers'environmental exposure. Existing traffic management strategies focus on travel efficiency, with limited attention to exposure risks. Taking mega-event travel as a short-term high-demand scenario, this study develops an exposure-aware multi-agent routing framework integrating road-network conditions, event-induced demand, background traffic, and environmental data within a unified simulation environment. Motorized travelers optimize travel efficiency, whereas micro-mobility travelers consider travel time and dynamic exposure to traffic-related PM2.5 and noise. We compare the framework with shortest-distance, congestion-aware, and exposure-aware routing baselines. Results show that, under high demand, the SARSA-based framework reduces vehicle travel time by 34.59% and cumulative environmental exposure by 58.65%, while micro-mobility travel time remains nearly unchanged. Exposure reduction is jointly driven by vehicle-side congestion mitigation and low-exposure routing. The framework provides quantitative support for vehicle diversion, low-exposure route guidance, and health-oriented traffic management in short-term high-demand scenarios.

Title: Learning Calibrated Confidence for Multi-Agent Collaboration
Authors: Chenxiao Fan, Chongming Gao, Gangyi Zhang, Yaxin Gong, Leyang Shen, Jiakai Wang, Dong Wang, Yang Liu, Haoyan Liu, Xinting Hu, Fuli Feng, Xiangnan He
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Multiagent Systems (cs.MA)
Abstract: Complex information seeking on the Web often requires collecting evidence from multiple documents and reasoning across them, as in multi-hop question answering. Multi-agent systems address such tasks by dividing work among specialized agents, where upstream agents produce intermediate answers and supporting evidence that downstream agents build upon. However, upstream answers vary in correctness, and most systems provide no quantitative signal about it, leaving the downstream agent to judge whether to trust or verify what it receives based solely on the textual evidence. In this paper, we propose MASCAL. Each agent learns to produce a correctness probability for its answer by jointly optimizing task performance and confidence calibration in reinforcement learning; the upstream agent passes this probability at handoff, giving the downstream agent a quantitative basis for its decisions, and the final answer also carries a calibrated probability, quantifying the reliability of the system output. To guide the downstream agent in using this signal during training, we introduce confidence-aware weighting, which increases the learning weight at positions responsive to the upstream probability, so that the agent learns more from decisions where it actively uses the signal. Across three collaboration architectures spanning Web retrieval and reasoning tasks, MASCAL improves task accuracy and calibration quality for both agents, and generalizes to deeper collaboration chains and different model scales. Intervention analysis confirms that upstream confidence affects downstream decision behavior, and the learned final confidence supports selective answering and targeted rechecking.

Title: Legal-R1: Agentic Retrieval for Evidence-Based Legal Reasoning
Authors: Huaiwen Pang, Jiale Han, Junying Chen, Wenjun Xiao, Benyou Wang
Abstract: Legal question answering requires answers that are not only plausible, but also grounded in legally valid and citable evidence. Standard retrieval-augmented generation often relies on one-shot semantic matching, which is insufficient when legal evidence must be selected according to authority, applicability, and diversity across heterogeneous sources. We introduce Legal-R1, an agentic retrieval framework for evidence-based legal reasoning. Legal-R1 decomposes legal reasoning into a multi-agent workflow, where a Lawyer agent learns when to retrieve, which legal source to query, what evidence to seek, and when the collected evidence is sufficient. A Legal Assistant agent retrieves from normative legal sources and precedent cases with authority-aware and diversity-aware selection, while a Judge agent generates the final answer from the complete evidence trajectory. We post-train only the Lawyer agent with masked supervised fine-tuning and trajectory-aware reinforcement learning. Experiments on multiple Chinese legal benchmarks show that Legal-R1 improves over general-purpose, legal-specific, and retrieval-augmented baselines.

Title: Can LLM Annotators Match Human Consistency? Benchmarking Human Agreement and Optimizing Multi-Agent with Contrastive Knowledge
Authors: Xiaopeng Ke, Zhixin Wang, Xuebo Liu, Xinyu Ma, Xing Zheng, Bowen Song, Weiqiang Wang, Min Zhang
Abstract: LLM-based annotation has advanced rapidly, yet existing benchmarks remain misaligned with real-world practice. Actual annotation often involves lengthy, task-specific guidelines, and different annotators may produce divergent but reasonable judgments, especially on boundary cases, where single-labeled dataset fail to reflect this disagreement. This gap also limits existing single-agent and workflow-based annotation systems, which often lack adaptability to complex, evolving guidelines. To bridge this gap, we introduce ANT-A Benchmark, a real-world multi-annotator benchmark spanning 7 datasets across domains and modalities, with task-specific guidelines and 5 independent human labels per instance. ANT-A enables a distribution-aware evaluation, using Fleiss kappa to assess how closely model annotations align with human labeling distributions. We further propose ANT-OR, a multi-agent annotation framework that refines prompts by distilling contrastive decision rules from positive and negative feedback. Experiments show that ANT-OR improves agreement@>=2 accuracy by 4.5 points over the strongest baseline and achieves the highest alignment with human annotator distributions as measured by Fleiss kappa within 2 points. Code and benchmark are available at https://github.com/Krueske/ANT-OR.

Title: DHCG: Dynamic Construction of Hierarchical Collaboration Graphs for LLM-Based Multi-Agent Reasoning
Authors: Jie Ren, Jiakang Yuan, Chenyu Huang, Hezeer Ma, Jiayuan Fan, Tao Chen
Abstract: LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) have demonstrated strong capabilities in solving complex problems across diverse domains. Recently, the dynamic orchestration of agent systems has become an important research direction. However, existing methods suffer from limited composition, misaligned dependencies, and inflexible scale, restricting their ability to adapt to reasoning requirements during execution. To address these limitations, we reframe MAS design as a partially observable Markov decision process, in which both the composition and scale of the MAS are dynamically determined. We propose DHCG, a novel framework that coordinates three modules (Planner, Worker, and Generator) to progressively construct a dynamic hierarchical collaboration graph from scratch based on the query and evolving execution feedback. At each step, guided by feedback, the Planner generates a set of distinct and complementary roles tailored to the current reasoning needs and selectively routes relevant information to each role. It can also finalize the hierarchical collaboration graph early or progressively expand it when additional reasoning is required. We further introduce action-aware preference optimization to train the Planner to make more effective decisions when constructing hierarchical collaboration graphs. We systematically evaluate DHCG across code generation, mathematical reasoning, and domain-specific reasoning benchmarks. DHCG achieves state-of-the-art average performance among the compared methods, improving over the single-agent baseline by 13.06 points and outperforming both static and dynamic MAS baselines by 2.77-8.02 points. Additional experiments further demonstrate its generalization across different Planner backbones and unseen Worker models.

Title: RaspAssistant as an Agentic Framework for Automating Adsorption Simulation Research in Porous Materials
Authors: Marko Petković, Susanne Gooijer, José Manuel Vicent-Luna, Vlado Menkovski, Sofía Calero
Abstract: Porous-material adsorption studies require coordinated structure preparation, force-field selection, simulation, validation, and interpretation, making end-to-end automation difficult. We test whether RaspAssistant, a hierarchical multi-agent framework, can carry an adsorption study from force-field preparation through validation and downstream separation analysis. Across twelve multi-agent workflow-reproduction runs spanning four adsorption and separation benchmarks, overall scores ranged from 8.50 to 10.00 on a rubric evaluating workflow correctness, simulation validity, and analysis consistency. In a separate eight-case force-field extraction benchmark, the mean weighted score was 0.967, combining parameter agreement and RASPA readiness. In open-ended studies, the system diagnosed and refined an acetylene force field and, after validating a CO$_2$ force field against MFI experiments, screened 197 pure-silica zeolites that passed automated input checks. These results demonstrate autonomous workflow execution after task specification and input provision: RaspAssistant coordinates, validates, adapts, and documents extended adsorption-simulation workflows while exposing model sensitivity and methodological limitations for expert review.

Title: Mind Your Own Role: Reducing Role Overstepping for Effective and Efficient Multi-Agent Collaboration via Dynamic Role Activation Steering
Authors: Xingke Yang, Sicong Li, Lingfeng Yao, Rui Chen, Gen Li, Hao Wang, Xin Fu, Miao Pan
Abstract: Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) have shown strong capability in solving complex tasks by assigning different agents specialized roles and corresponding subtasks. However, agents may overstep their assigned responsibilities and perform subtasks belonging to other roles, which can disrupt workflow, reduce system efficiency, and degrade task performance. To address this issue, we investigate role-related patterns in the model's internal activation space and uncover two key observations: (i) role instructions induce consistent directional shifts in activation space, and (ii) role-adherent and role-overstepping trajectories exhibit distinct activation patterns. Based on these observations, we propose Dynamic Role Activation Steering (DRAS), a lightweight and effective inference-time activation intervention approach to reduce role overstepping in multi-agent collaboration. Specifically, DRAS constructs a role steering vector and a lightweight role-overstepping detector for each role. During LLM generation, the detector estimates the probability of role overstepping from the current activation state, and DRAS dynamically adjusts the steering strength accordingly to guide the agent toward its assigned responsibilities. Experimental results show that DRAS effectively reduces the number of role-overstepping trajectories by up to 86.6% compared with Vanilla MAS, thereby improving task quality score by 10.0%--11.1%, achieving a 1.50$\times$--1.61$\times$ task-completion speedup, and reducing token consumption by 26.8%--38.7%.

Title: Thought Blocks: Non-Autoregressive Latent Communication for Multi-Agent Systems via Trajectory-to-State Compilation
Authors: Zhenhan Guan, Xiaolong Liu, Hengwei Ye, Zheng Tian
Abstract: LLM-based multi-agent systems typically communicate through text, incurring repeated generation and re-encoding costs. Although latent communication removes explicit verbalization, constructing latent messages may still require autoregressive latent trajectories. We therefore distinguish message representation from message construction and ask whether agents can directly construct useful continuation states without executing the trajectories that normally produce them. We formulate this problem as trajectory-to-state compilation and introduce Thought Blocks, fixed-size blocks of latent key--value (KV) continuation memory constructed in one shot. Thought Blocks achieve a 2.5 times average latency speedup over autoregressive latent communication. Compared with text-based multi-agent communication, Thought Blocks reduce text tokens by 45.7% and autoregressive steps by 84.8%, achieving an 8.6 times average latency speedup. These results demonstrate that trajectory-to-state compilation enables efficient inter-agent latent communication without sequential latent rollouts at inference.

Title: Towards High Semantic Fidelity: Hyperdimensional Symbolic Messages in Multi-Agent Communication
Authors: Shoucheng Song, Chang Yao, Hao Wu, Youfang Lin, Sheng Han, Kai Lv
Abstract: Semantic fidelity is essential for multi-agent communication under non-ideal channels, comprising transmission fidelity and conversion fidelity. Yet existing numerical and neural message formats cannot simultaneously achieve both. To address this, we propose a novel message format-\textbf{H}yperdimensional \textbf{S}ymbolic \textbf{M}essages (HSM) and its corresponding communication framework \textbf{Herm}. For transmission fidelity, Herm suppresses semantic entanglement via an entity-attribute-value structured encoding pipeline. For conversion fidelity, Herm first leverages a receiver-centric ego-binding mechanism to align semantics. Then, a similarity-aware dual-branch fusion module is proposed to prevent critical semantic dilution. To realize explicit message-semantic conversion, we devise an iterative decoding scheme via algebraic inverse operations. Experiments exhibit that Herm outperforms baselines across various noisy scenarios while maintaining superior structural readability.

Title: S$^2$-MAS: A Society-Scale Multi-Agent Simulation Framework with a 500-Million-Persona Resource
Authors: Yang Li, Yike Wang, Di Wan, Chujun He, Zongsi Xu, Yitao Yu, Shuai Zhong, Minghao Pan, Quanfeng Lu, Xiyu Chen, Sheng Zhong, Deng Binjie, Yichen Guo, Zhenwei Guo, Hou Jun, Kunhan Guo, Weihao Lin, Tuo Zhou, Hai Liu, Chenwei Wu, Jianyuan Zhong, Xilin Dai, Ye Luo
Abstract: Simulating economic responses at society scale requires decision rules that respond to household circumstances and accounting rules that track their consequences. We introduce S$^2$-MAS, a multi-agent simulation framework with a resource of 500 million synthetic household personas. It combines trainable candidate-scoring policies, reusable financial scenarios and explicit state transitions. Trained with SFT + RLCD on 2.93 million examples, YN-mini-MLX achieves 74.55% accuracy and 38.37% question-macro F1 on held-out consumer financial-choice tasks, improving on the training-question majority baseline by 2.78 and 6.21 percentage points. A completed application evaluates 12 million distinct households in two purchase-funding conditions: 24 million one-shot choices feed 288 million monthly ledger states in 3 h 59 min on 14 GPUs. Jointly increasing purchase goals and approved limits produces heterogeneous consumption, cash and repayment paths, with much of the consumption variation arising from transitions between deferral and purchase. In a separate 1,060-household retrospective consumption experiment, standalone YN-master-9B has 3.42% lower annual MAE than the deterministic fully rational benchmark, alongside a 19.7% lower predicted population mean than observed. Information-timing tests show how year labels and later outcome information change decisions. Together, these experiments establish an executable alternative for studying heterogeneous household behavior with learned policies and explicit financial accounting.

Title: DynaFlow: Learning Free-Form Multi-Agent Orchestration
Authors: Ruhao Liu, Qi Li, Shizun Wang, Xinchao Wang
Abstract: Multi-agent systems often rely on predefined collaboration structures, limiting their ability to adapt to diverse task requirements. We introduce DynaFlow, a framework that integrates free-form executable workflow synthesis into the action space of the main agent. The agent decides when collaboration is needed and generates task-specific programs that coordinate sub-agents through sequential or parallel execution, structured information exchange, and verification. Execution results and traces inform subsequent actions, enabling the agent to adapt collaboration as reasoning progresses. We train only the main agent through supervised fine-tuning on distilled trajectories, followed by refinement on examples filtered for unsupported premises, biased verification, and information-flow defects. All sub-agents remain fixed, separating orchestration learning from executor capability improvement. Across six benchmarks spanning mathematical reasoning, scientific question answering, and multi-hop retrieval, DynaFlow achieves 88.08% overall accuracy in Forced mode, outperforming the strongest evaluated baseline by 10.90 percentage points with the same Qwen3.5-27B backbone. Workflow analysis finds more explicit use, verification, and refinement of upstream outputs after training, highlighting cross-stage information flow as a key dimension of multi-agent orchestration.

Title: A Hyper-Logical View on Multi-Agent Path Planning
Authors: Hadar Frenkel, Dor Atzmon
Abstract: Multi-Agent Path Planning (MAPP) requires collision-free paths for multiple agents. MAPP has numerous real-life applications, including the navigation of automated vehicles, and has therefore many variants considering different constraints, requirements, and objectives. For each such variant, a new algorithmic treatment is often developed. This paper takes a complementary, specification-centered view: we show that many MAPP variants can be modeled in HyperLTL, a temporal logic that reasons about multiple paths and their evolution through time, and in its omega-regular extension HyperQPTL. The contribution is not a claim that current hyperproperty model checkers replace specialized MAPP solvers. Rather, the hyper-logical view gives a unified language for comparing MAPP variants, adding cross-agent constraints, expressing optimality, and connecting MAPP to verification, explanation, and causality techniques for hyperproperties.

Title: Replication or Corroboration? An Axiomatic Framework for Evidential Dependence in Multi-Agent Debate
Authors: Hoang-Loc Cao, Truong Thanh Hung Nguyen, Phuc Truong Loc Nguyen, Vo Thanh Khang Nguyen, Phuc Ho, Hung Nguyen, Duc Pham, Long Tran-Thanh, Hung Cao
Subjects: Multiagent Systems (cs.MA); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Logic in Computer Science (cs.LO)
Abstract: In multi-agent debates, matching reports can arise for two different reasons: agents may repeat the same evidence (replication), or they may provide separate evidential roots that support the same claim (corroboration). A judge must distinguish these two cases. Counting report occurrences gives extra weight to relays, paraphrases, alias resubmissions, and excerpt splits, while merging all matching content avoids this only by also removing genuine corroboration. We formalize this tension as a minimal judgment game in which acquiring new evidence is costly, but replication is cheap. We show that root replication invariance (RRI) is exactly threshold-uniform replication immunity. Under RRI, replication-only deviations cannot change the verdict, and positive-cost replication is strictly dominated, whereas occurrence-sensitive and content-keyed judges admit profitable deviations. We also establish an information boundary: if a judge's observation interface cannot distinguish a replica from a matched fresh root, no judge can both ignore the replica and respond strictly to the fresh root. To preserve this distinction, we introduce the lineage quotient, which removes wording, identity, occurrence multiplicity, and arbitrary root names while keeping distinct roots separate. On orbit-connected domains, it is the coarsest representation sufficient for every deterministic judge invariant to replication and root-label renaming. We further lift this construction to quantitative bipolar argumentation frameworks (QBAFs), characterize strict fresh-root response, prove its propagation along sign-consistent paths under DF-QuAD, and derive a tight closed-form response modulus. Exhaustive audits over 28,224 direct-star profiles, 2,052 multi-layer DAGs, with matched interventions on 277 AVeriTeC-derived profiles, show the predicted separation between replication and corroboration under a supplied partition.

Title: MAS-Loop: Beyond One-Shot Orchestration towards Self-Evolving Multi-Agent Systems
Authors: Hehai Lin, Qi Yang, Chengwei Qin
Abstract: Training-time multi-agent system (MAS) design seeks to learn reusable orchestration policies, yet prevailing approaches remain largely one-shot: an Orchestrator generates a system but only observes and learns from its terminal outcome. This paradigm discards execution trajectories that expose system-level failures and contain fine-grained information beyond the terminal outcome, leaving no direct basis for revising the source MAS, evaluating the updated MAS, or learning from the resulting contrast. To this end, we introduce MAS-Loop, an execution-grounded framework that closes this feedback loop by coupling an Orchestrator with a trajectory-conditioned Refiner. For each task, the Orchestrator constructs and executes a source MAS to obtain an outcome score and an intermediate trajectory. Conditioned on the trajectory, the Refiner localizes an actionable failure, formulates a trajectory-grounded diagnosis, and proposes a bounded patch to the agents, information flow, or execution configuration. The executable updated MAS is re-executed on the same task to measure its realized outcome under stochastic execution. This pair-MAS comparison provides complementary learning signals: the Orchestrator learns to generate strong systems with fewer recoverable failures, whereas the Refiner learns to expose and repair observed weaknesses, thereby driving policy-level co-evolution across training iterations. Experiments show that MAS-Loop achieves the strongest overall performance among the evaluated baselines, with consistent gains from refinement across all evaluated benchmarks. The co-evolution process also yields MAS-JudgeCorpus, a dataset of execution-grounded source-updated pairs with orchestration- and trajectory-level supervision, which can provide the community with support for MAS reward modeling and trajectory-aware investigation.

Title: MACTS-EM: Multi-Agent Collaborative Time Series Forecasting with Emergent Memory
Authors: Ahmad Shahi, Mamehgol Yousefi
Abstract: Time series forecasting remains a critical challenge across numerous domains. Despite significant advancements, existing approaches struggle with complex phenomena such as regime shifts, cross-domain knowledge transfer, and multimodal data integration. This paper introduces Multi-Agent Collaborative Time Series Forecasting with Emergent Memory (MACTS-EM), a novel framework where specialised agents collaborate to achieve superior forecasting performance. The MACTS-EM architecture integrates: (1) domain-specialised forecasting agents for pattern recognition, anomaly detection, causal inference, and uncertainty quantification; (2) a meta-cognitive layer for dynamic agent allocation; (3) an emergent memory mechanism enabling cross-domain pattern transfer; (4) multimodal contextual integration; and (5) adversarial robustness components. Evaluation across financial markets, climate patterns, energy consumption, and pandemic propagation demonstrates that MACTS-EM outperforms existing approaches in most scenarios, with 8-12% improvement in forecasting accuracy, 22-27% better zero-shot transfer capability, 16-21% enhanced resilience during regime shifts, and 15-18% faster recovery after distribution shifts. Our findings suggest that collaborative, agentic approaches to time series forecasting represent a promising direction beyond traditional architectures, particularly for complex real-world scenarios requiring multi-resolution temporal understanding and contextual adaptation.

Title: When Debate Helps: Proposal Supply and Verification-Aware Readout in Multi-Agent Reasoning
Authors: Zihao Zhao, Tunyu Zhang, Haizhou Shi, Yusong Zhao, Xinxi Zhang, Hao Wang
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computation and Language (cs.CL); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Multiagent Systems (cs.MA); Social and Information Networks (cs.SI)
Abstract: Multi-agent debate can improve reasoning, yet often fails to beat simple majority voting. We argue that successful debate requires two distinct mechanisms: proposal supply must surface a correct answer, and readout must identify that answer when voting misses it. We formalize the first requirement through recoverable headroom, which measures cases where a correct proposal is available but the majority answer is wrong. For the second, we develop Latent Verification Debate (LVD), an accounting model in which candidate proposals receive answer-specific verification evidence before final generation. Controlled fixed-proposal interventions estimate this latent effect in equivalent peer-support units and show that correct evidence changes answer probabilities and generated decisions while proposal supply remains fixed. To improve proposal supply, we construct societies from neural-thicket agents using labeled and label-free coverage objectives. Across two backbones and matched-budget reasoning benchmarks, coverage-selected societies increase complementary proposal supply and improve aggregate accuracy in repeated stochastic evaluations. Round-level controls further show that interaction provides gains beyond applying the same finalizer directly to the initial proposals. These results identify proposal coverage and truth-sensitive evidence use as complementary conditions for debate to outperform voting. Code is available at https://github.com/Wang-ML-Lab/when-debate-helps.

Title: LLM-Based Multi-Agent Collaboration for Constrained Multi-Objective Container Placement
Authors: Suvarthi Sarkar, Abhishek Hazra, Akshat Mittal, Aryabartta Sahu
Subjects: Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC); Multiagent Systems (cs.MA)
Abstract: Container placement in data centers must simultaneously minimize power consumption and maximize affinity preferences, while satisfying multi-resource capacity and anti-affinity constraints. Traditional approaches typically rely on fixed rules, which lack adaptability to dynamic cluster states and are difficult to extend for adaptive decision-making. On the other hand, meta-heuristic methods, although more flexible, are often computationally expensive, slower and prone to getting trapped in local optima. In this work, we propose an adaptive and efficient approach based on an LLM-driven multi-agent collaboration framework, where four specialized agents operate in a closed-loop ReAct cycle at each placement step. A Power Consumption Agent and an Affinity Agent debate over competing objectives, while a Placement Agent resolves conflicts using Tolerance-Gated Arbitration (TGA). A Rearrangement Agent further refines decisions through the Monotone Improvement Rule (MIR) in a post-placement refinement phase. All the agents reason over deterministic, feasibility-filtered candidate tables provided by the environment, ensuring that every proposed action inherently satisfies hard constraints. Based on experimental evaluation using the Google Cluster Trace with a configuration of 100 applications and 25 machines, the proposed framework consumes 8.36% less power and achieves 39.30% higher affinity than the power-greedy baseline, 7.12% less power and 10.85% higher affinity than the best domain-specific heuristic (HOP-CAPM), and 4.26% less power and 1.83% higher affinity than the meta-heuristic approach (CPAAP), averaged over three independent runs. Ablation studies confirm that each architectural component, the multi-round debate mechanism, the TGA in the Placement Agent, and the MIR in the Rearrangement Agent, contributes meaningfully to the overall performance, with removal of any single component degrading both power consumption and affinity satisfaction.
Venue: Int Conf Cloud Comput [services Soc, CLOUD, International Conference on Cloud Computing [Services Society], IEEE Int Conf Cloud Comput

Title: OA-MAP: Evidence-Grounded Multi-Agent Multimodal Framework for Interpretable Knee Osteoarthritis Progression
Authors: Sixu Chen, Mingrui Yang, Qiang Guan, Xiaojuan Li
Abstract: Knee osteoarthritis (KOA) progression prediction can support patient monitoring, requiring the integration of multimodal data and multidomain expertise. Moreover, isolated risk estimates provide limited insight underlying a prediction. To automate the progression assessment workflow and reduce manual effort while providing interpretable findings and supporting evidence, we present OA-MAP, an autonomous multi-agent framework for evidence-grounded assessment of structural and pain progression in KOA. The system incorporates modality-specific agents including MRI, X-ray, and clinical agents, together with a coordinator agent. This framework can autonomously recruit specialist agents, select tools for prediction and analysis, and retrieve literature as external evidence based on user request and available patient information. An uncertainty-informed human-in-the-loop mechanism enables clinicians to review and correct intermediate findings, triggering recomputation of affected results. We evaluate the prediction models using 600 participants from the FNIH Osteoarthritis Biomarkers Consortium cohort. On the test set of 100 participants, the fusion models achieve AUROCs of 0.80 for structural progression and 0.68 for pain progression. A case study illustrates how OA-MAP combines risk estimates with intermediate findings, cross-modal conflicts, literature support, and uncertainty indicators to support interactive review.

Title: CoEvoke: Evoking Multi-Agent Collaboration for Trajectory Collection
Authors: Lin Wu, Shu Yao, Yuheng Wang, Jingru Fan, Huatao Li, Yihan Li, Liu Yixuan, Cheng Liu, Jian Chang, Zeyu Zhao, Aohua Zhang, Huiying Zhao, Shuyuan Zhu, Chen Qian
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Multiagent Systems (cs.MA); Software Engineering (cs.SE)
Abstract: Training multi-agent collaboration requires trajectories of checking, feedback, and repair, yet task-solving rollouts may end in immediate approval or repeat unsuccessful attempts without useful correction. We introduce CoEvoke, a cross-domain framework that evokes these interactions during trajectory collection. Controlled perturbations create recoverable difficulties, while restricted reference-based guidance directs investigation. The resulting dataset contains 4,567 reconstructable trajectories over 4,130 software-engineering and reasoning tasks, linking public interactions to evidence, decisions, and task-native outcomes. Separate experiments over 2,287 same-task pairs show feedback increases of 47.72-100 percentage points across seven perturbation groups; guidance has smaller, model-dependent effects. With identical training tasks, decision-record counts, and updates, perturbation-enriched judge training improves ACPBench-Hard success from 35.38% to 42.12% (+6.73 points). SWE verifier training gains 7.60-9.40 points over interface-matched untrained references. Workflow and post-training evaluations preserve task-solving topology with unperturbed inputs and no private-reference guidance. These results support designing collection conditions to obtain corrective supervision that improves collaborative decisions with frozen solving agents.

Title: Beyond Perfect Teammates: Multi-Agent Collaboration with Unreliable Colleagues
Authors: Chen Huang, Yiyang Zhang, Yuhao Wu, Yang Deng, Wenxuan Zhang
Abstract: LLM-based multi-agent collaboration is increasingly used to solve complex tasks by dividing work among specialized agents and integrating complementary expertise. Yet existing systems and evaluations largely rest on an implicit perfect-colleague assumption: collaborators provide correct and complete information and respond promptly to requests. In realistic teamwork, however, collaborators may return information that does not answer the intended question, provide insufficient detail to support a decision, or fail to respond to a request. To separate task-solving competence from the ability to recover an unreliable evidence-gathering process, we introduce the Unreliable Colleagues Benchmark (UnCoBench), which organizes behavioral failures through Misaligned, Incomplete, and Missed settings. The main agent need to verify contextual correctness, diagnose information gap and track unresolved dependencies in order to obtain the correct evidence for solving the task. We also introduce a verifiable and scalable automated generation pipeline that pairs LLM-based scenario generation with executable checks of answer uniqueness and role necessity. Results across ten models show that similar reliable-setting performance can result in different robustness to unreliable evidence. Trace analysis reveals frequent omissions of corrective follow-up, and the recovery behavior involves inefficient waiting and redundant queries. These findings show that robust collaboration requires not only sound reasoning, but also targeted action to diagnose evidence failures, recover relevant information, and integrate it into decisions. Our data and source code are available at https://github.com/iNLP-Lab/UnCoBench.

Title: Cooperation Without Adaptation: LLM Agents in a Collective-Risk Dilemma
Authors: Trung-Kiet Huynh, Dao-Sy Duy-Minh, Chi-Nguyen Tran, Phu-Hoa Pham, Phu-Quy Nguyen-Lam, Le Hong Trang, The Anh Han
Subjects: Computer Science and Game Theory (cs.GT); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computation and Language (cs.CL); Multiagent Systems (cs.MA)
Abstract: Language-model agents are increasingly deployed to act on behalf of people in settings where individual decisions shape shared outcomes. We examine whether five production models adapt their contributions to changing risks and partner behaviour, or instead follow a relatively fixed strategy. In a collective-risk dilemma game (CRG), six players contribute to a shared pool over ten rounds; if the pool falls short of its target, a catastrophe may destroy their remaining resources. Four models contributed approximately an equal share at every positive risk level, and four of the five also contributed when risk was zero, even though contributing could not improve their payoff. Explicitly stating that only the agent's own payoff mattered reduced zero-risk contributions for most models, while a more neutral prompt did not. Several models correctly identified which action offered the higher expected payoff at different risk levels, yet their contributions changed little. Against fixed partners, no model consistently chose the payoff-maximising response, and in mixed-model groups, a single agent's shortfall in the final round could cause an otherwise successful group to fail. Payoff-based selection also depended on population composition: in a single six-agent group, it favoured the model that contributed least and reduced group success, whereas in larger, randomly mixed populations, it favoured an exact fair-share model at moderate and high risk. These findings show that cooperative self-play alone is not evidence of strategic adaptability. Consistent with a machine-behaviour approach, evaluations of agents in multi-agent systems should test how they respond to incentives, partner actions, and population composition.

Title: Neuro-Inspired Inhibitory Message Passing for Accurate and Token-Efficient Multi-Agent Reasoning
Authors: Nima H. Siboni, Magdalena Springer, Vahid Rostami
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computation and Language (cs.CL); Multiagent Systems (cs.MA)
Abstract: Multi-agent systems promise to solve problems by bringing together information beyond the reach of any individual agent. Retrieval and tool use can distribute this information across agents, making communication essential to collaboration. A central challenge is keeping crucial evidence visible in each agent's context as messages accumulate. Repeated information can crowd out rare, decisive evidence. Models of cortical circuits suggest a principle for addressing this imbalance: inhibition can selectively suppress shared inputs while preserving sensitivity to weaker signals. We adapt this principle into inhibitory message passing, a training-free communication router that cancels redundant evidence separately for each evidence sentence and receiver. Each round, it forwards evidence sentences restated in agents'messages, delivering each at most once to receivers whose own evidence lacks it and excluding the senders'reasoning and answers. Against standard message passing, accuracy in peer groups rose by 39-77 percentage points across three benchmarks, and tokens per run fell by 10-46%. Gains held across seven open models spanning four to thirty-two billion parameters and two commercial models, in groups up to sixty-four agents, and across multi-agent architectures including peer-to-peer, orchestrator-worker, and multilevel hierarchical organizations. These findings support a scalable design pattern for more accurate and token-efficient multi-agent reasoning.

Title: Agentic AI Orchestration Framework for Spatial Intelligence: Supply Chain Deployment
Authors: Constantinos Papantoniou, Brian Hilton
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Multiagent Systems (cs.MA); Software Engineering (cs.SE)
Abstract: Industrial spatial decisions are assembled across systems that share neither a reference frame nor an owner, and analysts spend substantial effort reconciling those systems rather than reasoning about space. This paper presents ANASSA, a reference architecture integrating structured reasoning, multi-agent workflow orchestration, authoritative spatial grounding, and feedback-driven execution, and reports its instantiation in an operating supply-chain deployment. The architecture places typed data contracts at agent boundaries, validates spatial claims against a certified authoritative foundation, and enforces two blocking human-in-the-loop approvals inside a six-step cognitive loop. The deployment covers multi-hazard risk assessment on an ocean-and-inland freight lane, including cold-chain excursion detection over container telemetry. Across a three-month proof of concept (POC) with three implementation iterations, three deployment outcomes are reported: 25% improvement in data quality, 50% reduction in spatial workflow runtime, and 60% lower decision latency relative to the preceding manual workflow. Absolute deployment-scale quantities and baseline counts are confidential; reported percentages are observed relative changes. These are uncontrolled deployment observations, not controlled experiments. We therefore specify instrumentation and ablation protocols for mechanism-level evaluation.

Title: PCM: A Proof-Carrying Message Protocol for Verifiable Multi-Agent Communication
Authors: Bravish Ghosh (Cygnux Labs)
Subjects: Computational Engineering, Finance, and Science (cs.CE); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Cryptography and Security (cs.CR); Multiagent Systems (cs.MA)
Abstract: When one AI agent tells another that"the tests passed"or"a person approved this refund", the receiver has only the sender's word. A2A and MCP authenticate the channel, but the sender is the party in doubt, so a prompt-injected agent can launder fabricated facts and authority through a multi-agent system. We present Proof-Carrying Messages (PCM), a protocol in which each claim carries evidence: records from an append-only Merkle log that the agent cannot write, with inclusion proofs, signed by an attesting signer the agent cannot control. Receivers check messages offline and give each claim a three-valued result: proven, unproven or failed. A claim that rests only on the agent's own report is never proven. Authority travels as grant chains rooted in a recorded human approval, and the chains can only narrow. We specify four claim types, a typed caveat algebra, replay rules that survive restarts, and strict readings that make independent verifiers agree, and we prove the resulting security properties. On a pre-specified benchmark of 926 messages from real runs, 712 of them lies in 16 classes, PCM accepts 10 lies, all of them stale evidence (1.4%, 95% CI 0.8-2.6%). Plain A2A accepts all 712, and models of six deployed protocols (A2A with signed Agent Cards, uAgents, RFC 9421, SCITT, AP2, Verifiable Intent) accept 504-712. Two independent verifiers agree on all 926 verdicts, and verification takes about 1 ms.

Title: Right Answers, Wrong States: Hidden Information Failures in Multi-Agent Collaboration
Authors: Herun Wan, Jiaying Wu, Minnan Luo, Zihan Ma, Fanxiao Li, Nancy F. Chen, Min-Yen Kan
Abstract: Multi-agent systems are often judged by whether they reach the correct answer. This can miss a distinct failure: collaboration may leave behind a corrupted information state even when the immediate decision is correct. We call this an off-query failure. To study this failure in collaborative decision support, we introduce OffQuery, which separately evaluates evidence verification (T1), shared-state reconstruction (T2), and task resolution (T3) in two representative high-stakes settings: healthcare and disaster response. Across GPT, Gemini, and Qwen models, standard collaboration shows much stronger task performance than state reliability. Averaged over 21 model--setting combinations, task resolution reaches 64.7%, while evidence verification and state reconstruction reach only 14.3% and 43.1%. We trace this gap to selective information use: current queries often bypass corrupted facts, which become consequential when later tasks require them. We further introduce ReGround, which resolves conflicting evidence, verifies shared facts, reconstructs a trusted state, and reasons over that state. Across seven models from three families, ReGround improves all three capabilities in every evaluated setting, with average relative gains of 309.0%, 82.9%, and 17.6% on T1, T2, and T3. Reliable collaboration therefore requires both a correct decision and a reliable shared state for future reasoning.

Title: Harness-Search: Guiding Long-Horizon Search through Multi-Agent Coordination
Authors: Shanyong Wang, Zhenwen Ji, Lei Jin, Yining Zhao, Yicheng Qian, Chengqiang Lu, Yi Wu, Yao Hu, Lizhen Cui, Yanyu Xu
Abstract: Long-horizon search requires agents to gather evidence across multiple steps and synthesize it into well-supported answers. The recent agent harnesses provide a natural and promising framework to support such long-running search processes. As interaction histories grow, one single agent in harnesses might get stuck and cause the policy to lose track of unresolved questions, overlook useful evidence, or terminate before sufficient support has been collected. One of promising way is to decouple three distinct responsibilities of proposing retrieval actions, updating persistent state, and deciding when to stop rather than concentrating them within a single policy. Targeted at it, we introduce Harness-Search, a multi-agent search harness to reduce the local errors propagating across subsequent exploration, evidence curation, and termination decisions. In particular, Harness-Search assigns these responsibilities to three permission-bounded authorities: a Retrieval Policy that proposes search operations, a Memory Operator that validates and commits persistent-state updates, and a Summary Auditor that accepts or rejects termination based on the sufficiency of the curated evidence. Together, these roles form a Propose-Commit-Audit loop in which actions are proposed, persistent evidence is selectively committed, and stopping decisions are subjected to an explicit sufficiency check. Across seven long-horizon search benchmarks, Harness-Search improves both retrieval and answer generation under the same policy backbone, increasing Recall by 4.60-27.92 points and Final-Answer Recall by 12.34-30.13 points over the strongest harness-based baseline on each evidence-retrieval benchmark. Moreover, trajectory-level analyses show that Harness-Search continues to accumulate useful evidence and expand evidence coverage with less redundant retrieval as the search history grows.

Title: Constitutional Gating and Deterministic Recovery for Multi-Agent LLM Negotiation: Ablations Against a Stateful Adversarial Gatekeeper
Authors: Masaaki Nakatsu (AO, Inc. / OrbLabs AG), Reno Wang (AO, Inc.)
Abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems negotiating with a stateful counterpart waste model calls in three ways: polite loops that never meet the counterpart's hidden acceptance condition, malformed outputs that trigger retries, and compliance deadlocks in which the counterpart demands something the agent must refuse. We study a three-part control stack - a 5-Pillar runtime constitution, a 4-tier swarm (Director, three-agent majority vote, Monitor, schema hard gate) and Cognitive Annealing (deterministic deadlock detection, atomic purge of the agent-side context, a canonical recovery message) - against a released adversarial Gatekeeper whose acceptance rules are fixed regular expressions and whose LLM only renders reply text. The testbed has a known solution: it measures whether the stack executes a constitution-aligned strategy against swarm drift and recovers from deadlock, not whether it discovers anything. In five runs per configuration (30 runs; Gemini 2.5 Pro agents, Claude Haiku 4.5 Gatekeeper) we find: (i) the constitution and Director make an acceptable framing possible but not reliable - 0/5 baseline unlocks versus 1/5 and 2/5 with the constitution; when the swarm unlocks it does so in one turn with 7-8 calls and about 15k tokens (67-73% below baseline); when it does not, it costs 17-38% more; (ii) the Monitor and hard gate do not reduce unlocks and leave an audit trail; (iii) under a honeytrap-to-compliance deadlock, LLM-only steering escapes 0 of 5 times while atomic purge plus a canonical strike escapes 5 of 5 (Fisher $p = 0.008$) at the same call budget, with zero calls for the strike. LLM-written strikes failed the deterministic pre-flight 5 of 5 times although an LLM Monitor had approved four. Pre-registered hypotheses on average call and token reduction were not supported. Cost is bounded in every arm by deterministic stop rules; the stack adds recovery at no extra model cost.

Title: From Agents to Edges: Paired Optimization for Multi-Agent Collaboration
Authors: Feng Lin, Xiaotian Yu, Yifan Yang, Aijun Li
Abstract: Strong individual agents do not guarantee effective collaboration. Communication must align what one agent conveys with how another interprets and uses it. This dependency makes the communication edge a natural unit of optimization. We introduce Paired Automated Communication Optimization (PACO), which jointly optimizes the instructions at both ends of each edge and their shared communication convention in systems built on black-box language models. PACO keeps model weights, agent roles, and workflow topology fixed. A state-aware discounted bandit selects edges for refinement, while execution feedback guides paired revisions evaluated through staged end-to-end execution. The optimized instructions integrate into existing agent prompts without additional model calls at deployment. On a four-agent workflow evaluated across diverse multi-agent benchmarks, PACO consistently outperforms leading prompt-optimization and communication baselines. Configurations learned on HotpotQA retain their advantage in cross-dataset transfer without target-specific optimization. These results demonstrate that optimizing how agents communicate can substantially improve collaboration within an otherwise fixed system.

Title: MultiAgent-OPD: End-to-End Training of Hierarchical Multi-Agent Systems with On-Policy Distillation
Authors: Yuhan Sun, Jiaxin Zhao, Yongdong Luo, Yibo Hu, Meiguang Jin, Junfeng Ma, Weixun Wang, Weihang Pan, Zhongan Bi
Abstract: In a hierarchical multi-agent system, a Leader assigns tasks and subagents carry them out. Jointly training the Leader and the subagents is difficult because a final answer gives only indirect feedback to the subagents. An LLM judge can score the performance of the subagents, but these scores depend on the judge's own assessment of the quality of subagents'responses. We present MultiAgent-OPD, which combines on-policy distillation with reinforcement learning to jointly train a shared-parameter Leader-Searcher-Answerer team end to end. We first train a Teacher in a Searcher-Answerer workflow using answer correctness. During team training, the frozen Teacher scores student-generated search and summary tokens to provide local process supervision for the Searchers, while the Leader learns from team success and the Answerer from candidate correctness. Across seven datasets, the trained system reaches 38.68% macro avg@4, exceeding Prompted Critic by 4.06 percentage points and C-MAS + RL, the trained cascaded multiagent system, by 2.61 percentage points. The team also solves more questions within four attempts.

Title: CuratorMAS: Automating Dataset Curation via Multi-Agent Orchestration
Authors: Yixin Zhang, Wenjie Feng
Abstract: High-quality datasets are essential for reliable machine learning, but dataset curation remains costly and hard to generalize across domains. Existing methods typically rely on manually designed heuristics or model-dependent signals, limiting their applicability across tasks and user queries. To address these limitations and automate data curation, we propose \textbf{CuratorMAS}, a multi-agent collaboration framework that orchestrates agents to evaluate and curate high-quality datasets. To achieve the goal of flexible curation, CuratorMAS decomposes the complex curation process into five programmable execution stages and forms a parallelizable workflow. Specifically, CuratorMAS first performs dataset exploration to collect contextual information such as file structures and constraint cues, thereby developing a comprehensive understanding of the given task. In order to acquire up-to-date information, CuratorMAS retrieves domain knowledge from online sources to augment the evaluation process. Next, CuratorMAS derives the necessary evaluation criteria and computes the corresponding metrics. Based on these results, CuratorMAS executes filtering accordingly. Finally, an evolution module summarizes the evaluation outcomes and updates the relevant skills. Extensive and comprehensive experiments demonstrate that CuratorMAS significantly reduces the noise rate by up to 36.03 percentage points (pp) while also improving the F1 score of downstream models by up to 8.88 pp.

Title: Decoupled Multi-Agent Orchestration
Authors: Xinle Wu, Yao Lu
Abstract: Learned orchestration can automatically construct effective language-model multi-agent systems, but existing approaches couple planning to fixed worker pools and train decomposition and collaboration from the same terminal outcome, limiting transfer and obscuring credit assignment. We introduce DeOrch, which separates worker-agnostic planning from concrete worker selection.
