Authors: Yi Wen, Derong Xu, Pengyue Jia, Yichao Wang, Yingyi Zhang, Maolin Wang, Junyi Li, Wenlin Zhang, Xiaopeng Li, Yong Liu, Xiangyu Zhao
Abstract: The memory capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) have garnered increasing attention recently. Despite great success achieved, existing retrieval-based memory approaches typically overlook the differences between memories and employ a unified strategy to process all memories, leading to suboptimal performance. Thus, an intuitive question arises: can we categorize memory into different types and select appropriate strategies? However, given the topic-rich, scenario-complex, and boundary-blurred nature of memory scenarios, achieving precise classification of memories is not easy. To address this challenge, we propose a memory multi-class dataset in this paper, termed TriMEM, which provides precise annotations for memory types across diverse scenarios. Building upon this foundation, we propose a novel memory framework, named MemoType, which can adaptively recognize each memory and query type with the learned router model. With the memory and query routing, MemoType can retrieve the memory with corresponding query types and design tailored retrieval strategies, thereby enhancing the retrieval performance. Moreover, we theoretically prove that any single retrieval strategy is subject to a fundamental upper bound on its expected retrieval precision in multi-class corpora, leading to systematic precision degradation. Extensive experiments on three datasets demonstrate that MemoType consistently outperforms existing methods, achieving up to 16.18% improvement in Recall@1.

Title: Heterogeneous Agentic Coevolution
Authors: Wenqian Ye, Ziwei Guan, Zi Yang, Shivani Modi, Cici Cong Wu, Yunlong He, Yuxin Chen, Zhengyu Zhang, Liang Luo, Venkatesh Ranganathan, Jianhui Sun, Yantao Yao, Wenlin Chen, Buyun Zhang, Ellie Dingqiao Wen, Henry Kautz, Aidong Zhang
Abstract: Recent advances in self-improving LLM agents have demonstrated the potential of AI systems that drive their own intelligence. However, many domain-specific applications rely on specialized foundation models that possess strong domain expertise but remain dependent on human-designed improvements. Extending recursive self-improvement to these models presents a key challenge: as a specialist improves, the strategies used to advance it must also adapt. To address this challenge, we propose Heterogeneous Agentic CoEvolution (HACE), a framework that jointly evolves specialized foundation models and LLM agents through reciprocal learning. HACE improves the specialist through supervised learning while training the agent with on-policy reinforced self-training, guided by verified performance gains on the current specialist. The agent's exploration, in turn, informs subsequent specialist training, enabling both models to adapt to each other's progress. To sustain this reciprocal learning, HACE further employs evolutionary search to optimize their interaction harness, adapting how the models exchange information and select training experiences as their capabilities evolve. We evaluate HACE across three challenging domains: recommendation systems, protein function prediction in biology, and crystal stability prediction in material discovery. We show that HACE outperforms the evaluated self-improving methods on the primary task metrics across all three domains. These results shed light on heterogeneous coevolution as a universal approach to improving specialized foundation models through reciprocal interaction with a learning agent.

Title: SyntaxBench: A Statistical Diagnostic Framework for Character-Level Reasoning in Large Language Models
Authors: Mohsen Larni (1), Sobhan Ebrahimi Azar (1), Pouyan Nahed (1), Kazem Taghva (1) ((1) Department of Computer Science, University of Nevada, Las Vegas)
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
Abstract: Large language models are increasingly used where small syntactic errors matter, yet character-level reasoning is still evaluated mostly through isolated probes and aggregate accuracy. We introduce SyntaxBench, a diagnostic benchmark and statistical evaluation framework for character-level reasoning. It contains five core tasks, character counting, letter containment, palindrome detection, edit distance, and longest-string selection, plus index_to_span, a harder substring-extraction stress test. The five core tasks use paired English and character-length-matched random-string inputs. index_to_span documents share a 200-500 word band and are not character-length matched. All six tasks use zero-, one-, and four-shot prompts. We evaluate eight open-weight models from 2B to 32B parameters across 11 reasoning-mode configurations. The framework reports exact-match and relaxed accuracy, Cohen's kappa, paired McNemar tests with odds ratios, bootstrap confidence intervals, Kendall's tau, class-conditional metrics, tokenization analysis, and multiple-comparison-corrected tests. Three findings stand out. First, tokenization shapes accuracy: random strings are more character-visible than English strings (1.892 vs. 3.169 characters per token), and character-counting accuracy falls as English words occupy more tokens. Second, reasoning mode is not uniformly helpful: Gemma4-31B is nearly unchanged across modes on the near-saturated tasks, while Qwen3.6-27B is worse with thinking on palindrome detection (0.952 non-thinking vs. 0.886 thinking at four-shot). Third, index_to_span remains largely unsolved; the best four-shot exact-match accuracy is 6.75%. Character-level evaluation needs controlled inputs, paired tests, and analyses of tokenization and reasoning mode rather than aggregate accuracy alone.

Title: Specialized Decision Models vs. General-Purpose LLMs: Benchmarking Jev Across Knowledge, Reasoning, and Multilingual Tasks
Authors: Xing Li, Qingcheng Chang, Jinzhong Ning, Changfeng Xu, Shenlong Zhang, Yijia Zhang, Ling Luo, Hongfei Lin
Abstract: Jev is a"System One"model that returns a choice among given options instead of generating text. We study how such a specialized decision model compares with general-purpose large language models (LLMs). We evaluate Jev on 13 multiple-choice benchmarks covering knowledge, reasoning, and multilingual understanding, and compare it with 19 LLMs in three tiers: frontier, representative, and small. Jev is competitive with frontier LLMs on knowledge and commonsense benchmarks and obtains the best score on MMLU-Redux and ARC-Challenge. Outside mathematics, it also outperforms most representative LLMs and all small LLMs. However, it falls behind on mathematical word problems: on MathQA, it is 17.7 points below the frontier median and scores lower than all 19 LLMs. These results indicate that a specialized decision model can match general-purpose LLMs on decisions that rely mainly on knowledge, but not on decisions that require multi-step calculation.

Title: Query Your Way Out: Benchmarking Multi-Turn Knowledge Reasoning through Generalized Puzzle Solving
Authors: Xin Cheng, Junming Yang, Ning Xu
Abstract: Puzzles offer a natural testbed for Large Language Models (LLMs) reasoning because they pose verifiable goals under partial information and require multi-step decisions to reach a solution. However, existing puzzle benchmarks typically focus on narrow environments with rigid mechanics and tightly constrained solution targets. To bridge this gap, we introduce the Active Probing Benchmark (APB), which generalizes puzzle-solving by casting concept identification as an interactive reasoning task that integrates specialized knowledge assessment into the puzzle setting. Specifically, APB evaluates whether models can acquire information via multi-turn active probing and inference to pinpoint 960 target concepts of specialized difficulty across eight diverse academic domains. Our evaluation reveals a counter-intuitive phenomenon: most open-source reasoning models significantly underperform their standard instruction counterparts. This finding suggests that in interactive settings, these models struggle to leverage procedural reasoning to reliably access and apply specialized domain knowledge. Beyond these empirical insights, APB provides a scalable pipeline for generating benchmarks that probe knowledge reasoning under interaction across diverse settings.

Title: Are We Testing Too Much? A Survey of Benchmark Compression for Efficient Evaluation of Large Language Models
Authors: Guoming Ling, Yupei Lin, Zhongzhan Huang, Junxin Li, Junjie Liu, Shanshan Zhong, Hefeng Wu, Liang Lin
Abstract: Benchmarks are essential for evaluating and improving large language models (LLMs). Yet many widely used benchmarks are redundant, making evaluation unnecessarily expensive. Benchmark compression lowers this cost by estimating full-benchmark scores and rankings from a partial evaluation. Research in this area has grown rapidly since 2024, but to our knowledge no survey has systematically organized its methods and findings. We review 119 papers to explain how methods choose what to evaluate, recover full-benchmark results, and verify their reliability. From this analysis, we develop a taxonomy covering compression within individual benchmarks, across benchmark suites, and during adaptive evaluation, together with work on redundancy and reliability. We compare their information needs, total costs, reliability checks, and limitations. Methods reduce evaluation costs by selecting representative subsets, using cheaper or reusable information, and testing adaptively, but risk poor coverage, inaccurate estimates, and sequential delays. The resulting taxonomy and practical guide help researchers choose, validate, and deploy methods for more efficient and reliable LLM evaluation.

Title: BANGLAPLAN: A Benchmark for Constraint-Based Planning and Decision-Making in Bangla
Authors: Md Rayhanul Masud, S M Maksudul Alam, Mohammad Jaminur Islam
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly help users arrange appointments, plan journeys, and allocate limited resources. These tasks require models to satisfy constraints on time, cost, capacity, and order, or determine that no feasible solution exists. Bangla is the world's seventh most widely spoken language, and existing benchmarks cover many language and reasoning tasks. However, benchmarks for evaluating planning and decision-making in Bangla under explicit constraints remain lacking. We introduce BANGLAPLAN, a benchmark of 1,000 problems across ten task families grounded in everyday life and institutions in Bangladesh. It includes feasible and infeasible problems in four language registers: everyday, formal, colloquial, and Bangla--English mixed. Answers cover eight structured types, including schedules, routes, allocations, and ordered steps, in a common JSON format. We construct the benchmark through language-model-assisted drafting and independent human validation. We evaluate 11 open-weight and proprietary model configurations using exact match, separately reporting feasible-case accuracy, infeasibility detection, and format errors. We find a large performance gap: GPT-6.1 Sol achieves 98.7% accuracy and Qwen3.5-27B with thinking reaches 80.3%, while direct-answer configurations score at most 30.9%. Seven of eleven configurations perform below the always-``infeasible''baseline. Our findings also suggest that harder problems primarily reduce plan-construction accuracy, while infeasibility detection remains more robust. BANGLAPLAN provides a reproducible basis for evaluating planning and decision-making in Bangla. BANGLAPLAN is available at: https://github.com/mrayhanulmasud/banglaplan.

Title: From Triage to Impact: A Multi-Hop Reasoning Benchmark for Explainable Persian Hate Speech
Authors: Ghazal Kalhor, Sima Kamandloo, Mehrsa Shamsian, Behnam Bahrak
Abstract: Hate speech has become increasingly prevalent on social media, raising concerns about its detection, interpretation, and moderation. Persian, a relatively low-resource language, lacks sufficient annotated data and computational resources for fine-grained hate speech analysis. In this study, we introduce a fine-grained, multi-hop benchmark for explainable Persian hate speech analysis, covering content triage, target identification, hate tactic and moral foundation analysis, textual evidence extraction, harmful narrative inference, and severity assessment. By evaluating state-of-the-art large language models (LLMs), we find that performance generally declines as tasks require more fine-grained semantic and inferential reasoning. Proprietary models generally outperform open-weight models, while reasoning-oriented models show no consistent advantage. Incorporating intermediate reasoning steps substantially improves severity prediction compared with one-shot assessment. Our analysis further reveals that Incitement to Violence or Harm is most strongly associated with higher severity, while political-affiliation targets are particularly associated with subversion-based moral framing. Overall, this work provides insights into LLM-based hate speech analysis and supports more accountable moderation of Persian-language social media. The benchmark is publicly available at https://github.com/kalhorghazal/From-Triage-to-Impact.

Title: Muse Glimmer 30B: An On-Device Agentic Model
Authors: Arash Ebrahim Abtahizadeh, Muna Aghamelu, Adil Ahmed, Juan C. Angeles Acuna, Alexis Audran-Reiss, Asaf Avrahamy, Yoram Bachrach, Can Balioglu, Amar Budhiraja, Onur Çelebi, Gaurav Chaurasia, Joy Chen, Lynn Cherif, Lucia Cipolina-Kun, Gal Cohen, Timothée Darcet, Beto de Paola, Digant Desai, Sam Devlin, Derek Dunfield, Ivan Evtimov, Maryam Fazel-Zarandi, Rob Fergus, Jean-Christophe Gagnon-Audet, Grant Gardner, Bhavul Gauri, Paris Giampouras, Sujan Kumar Gonugondla, Antoine Grosnit, Young Han, Michael Hassid, Monuril Islam, Masoud Jalili Sabet, Songhao Jia, Narine Kokhlikyan, Svetlana Kurtsman, Sandra Lefdal, Chee Hau Leow, Noam Levi, Mike Lewis, Sanae Lotfi, Xiyang Luo, Despoina Magka, Saeed Mahloujifar, Neal Mangaokar, Ishita Mediratta, Alexander H. Miller, Hela Momand, Saba Nazir, Kelvin Niu, Mattia Opper, Parth Pathak, Alberto Pepe, Danielle Pintz, Mikhail Plekhanov, Sidhartha Reddy Potu, Anton Protopopov, Shengyi Qian, Shashank Rajput, Joseph Rocca, Scott Roy, Luca Sbordone, Amin Shakeri, Tatiana Shavrina, Michael Shvartsman, Ruan Silva, Anya Sims, Eric Michael Smith, Hugo Touvron, Mabel Ubong, Isabel Urrego, Yanzheng Xiang, Zhiyuan Yao, Alex Yarmula, He Ye, Jade Yu, Luke Zettlemoyer, Arman Zharmagambetov, Perpetua Fathima Ahlijah, Tremo Ahmed, Enrique Alfonseca, Pedram Bashiri, Nikolay Bashlykov, Amine Benhalloum, Aaron Berman, Rohith Bhatia, Siddharth Bhattacharya, Prashant Bhende, Chloe Bi, Shuchao Bi, Clement Anthonioz Blanc, Allen Bolourchi, Iva Simon-Bubalo, Pere-Lluís Huguet Cabot, Andrea Caciolai, Erica Cai, Xiang Tony Cao, Yue Cao, Andrew Caples, Jinzhao Chang
Abstract: We introduce Muse Glimmer, an open-source 30B parameter causal language model with perception encoder, purpose-built for autonomous agentic tasks on consumer hardware. Muse Glimmer integrates multi-step reasoning, reliable tool use and failure recovery into a single model that runs locally on consumer devices without requiring cloud infrastructure. The model accepts text and image inputs and produces text outputs, was trained on data from over a hundred languages, and is quantized to approximately 4-bit precision for efficient single-GPU inference. Muse Glimmer achieves state-of-the-art performance for its size class on agentic benchmarks, setting a new standard compared to the models of its size: Gemma4-31B and Qwen3.6-27B on tool use, multi-step planning, and agentic task completion. We release the model under the Apache 2.0 license to foster open-source development of capable, safe, local AI agents.

Title: From Questions to Queries to Insights: A Schema-Grounded Agentic Workflow for Natural-Language Crash Data Analysis
Authors: Jingwen Zhu, Keshu Wu, Steven T. Parker, Bin Ran, David A. Noyce
Abstract: Transportation agencies maintain extensive crash databases to identify safety priorities, evaluate countermeasures, and guide resource allocation. Making these data accessible to practitioners requires flexible ways to translate analytical questions into reliable results. Existing dashboards support predefined analyses, while additional requests often depend on specialists who understand database queries, coded fields, and agency conventions. This study presents CrashDB-QA, a fully local, schema-grounded agentic workflow that enables natural-language analysis of crash databases. Specialized components interpret questions, generate and validate read-only SQL, execute queries, and explain the results. A shared knowledge base grounds query construction in the agency's data dictionary and safety-analysis conventions, while recorded intermediate outputs support inspection and auditing. An optional extension, CrashDB-QA+, checks the alignment among the question, query, and execution result and supplies evidence for iterative repair. We evaluate the workflow on a frozen snapshot of 4.4 million Wisconsin crash records using a new benchmark of 300 questions across ten analytical categories and nine local open-weight models. Domain grounding substantially improves query accuracy, and a code-specialized 7B model provides the best accuracy-latency balance among the tested models. Compositional analyses remain more difficult than routine retrieval, particularly comparisons between groups or periods. Verification improves performance when the Judge uses authoritative field definitions and the Refiner receives execution evidence, whereas additional checking alone offers no consistent benefit. These findings demonstrate the potential of locally deployed, domain-grounded workflows to broaden access to crash analysis and identify the reasoning and verification capabilities needed for reliable use.

Title: The Cost of a Hop: Benchmarking NLIP and A2A
Authors: Ranjan Sinha, Anindita Das, Ashika Anand Babu, Hari Palleti
Abstract: Autonomous agents built on Large Language Models (LLMs) need standardized protocols to interoperate across systems. Several now exist (A2A, MCP, ACP, ANP, NLIP), but the Natural Language Interaction Protocol (NLIP) has not appeared in any controlled performance study, and no work has measured where an agent protocol's latency is spent. We compare NLIP and the Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol empirically, decomposing latency into message creation, connection, and send phases across three independent hardware environments. For lightweight coordination, NLIP is 8.4-9.6x faster than the baseline A2A SDK implementation on two environments and about 4x on a third; the direction of the advantage is consistent, its magnitude depends on the hardware. The advantage is stage-specific: for the end-to-end pipeline, where LLM inference dominates, the protocols are near parity. The difference comes almost entirely from connection setup. To test A2A at its best, we also ran A2A SDK with connection caching enabled; caching narrows its gap with NLIP by a hardware-dependent amount, from 2.75x on one machine to near-parity on faster hardware, where at scale a cache-optimized A2A-SDK matches NLIP. We report these as measured conditions without a single causal account of the residual send-phase cost. Against the more optimized Python-A2A, NLIP leads by about 4x on the same stage. We close with a protocol-selection guide keyed to workload characteristics.

Title: Agentic discovery of blood biomarker from distilled private health records
Authors: Seffi Cohen, Liat Antwarg Friedman, Amir Anisman, Ruth Johnson, Michelle M. Li, Ayush Noori, Ben Reis, Ran Balicer, Noa Dagan, Marinka Zitnik
Abstract: Routine complete blood counts (CBCs) could yield new biomarkers, but the private records needed to evaluate candidates cannot be shared with frontier language model agents that excel at discovery. We distilled the evidence held in the Clalit Health Services panel of over 5.4 million patients into a released scoring tool: for each of 13 immune-mediated diseases, a graph attention network was trained inside the data boundary to predict the case-control AUC of candidate CBC expressions, and only the trained weights were released. The tool grounds an agent's propose-score-refine loop in real-world data without exposing any patient data. In external validation, agent-discovered expressions improved on their literature-seeded starting points by a median of 4.18 AUC percentage points, and across three independent cohorts, reranking the candidates of three frontier research tools improved on their first choices in most comparisons, with gains that varied by cohort. The released scorer supports privacy-preserving biomarker hypothesis generation.

Title: Beyond Imitation: A Framework and Benchmark for LLM-Assisted Peer Review
Authors: Rachel S.Y. Teo, Yutaro Yamada, Shashank Kotyan, Yuki Imajuku, Tarin Clanuwat
Abstract: The rapid growth of scientific publishing has strained peer review, particularly in machine learning, raising concerns about declining review quality and increasing reviewer workload. Large language models (LLMs) have been proposed as automated review assistants, yet their evaluation has focused largely on imitating human-written reviews rather than supporting the core functions of peer review. Here, we introduce a verification-centric perspective on LLM-assisted peer review, emphasizing error detection as a critical and resource-intensive task. We present a scalable benchmark that evaluates review systems'ability to identify logical contradictions, constructed through synthetic insertion of errors into conference papers, yielding unambiguous evaluation targets and enabling systematic comparison. We further propose a Multi-Layered Review (MLR) framework that prioritizes detailed manuscript comprehension before review generation, aligning more closely with human reviewing practices while improving token efficiency. Across evaluations, our approach demonstrates strong alignment with human review scores, achieves high error detection performance, and provides complementary perspectives on reviewer focus. These improvements can be attributed to both the choice of the underlying LLM and the design of our system. At the same time, we corroborate persistent vulnerabilities to adversarial manipulation, underscoring the need for robustness in automated review systems. Our findings highlight the importance of rigorous, error-focused evaluation to guide responsible deployment of LLM-based tools in peer review and other critical scientific workflows.

Title: Mind the Spatial Gap: A Benchmark for Geospatial Reasoning and Constrained Spatial Editing
Authors: Zheng Ren, Yanning Wang, Ziheng Huang, Fei Huang, Shiqi Wang, Ziqian Ye, Yang Yue
Abstract: Understanding and manipulating spatial relations is fundamental to AI systems that reason about physical environments and construct grounded world models. However, existing evaluations of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) for spatial reasoning rely predominantly on static question-answering (QA) over small-scale or synthetic scenes, rarely probing whether models can modify spatial configurations while satisfying explicit geometric constraints. We introduce GeoSpatialBench, a benchmark designed to evaluate an escalating progression of spatial cognition, ranging from spatial relation understanding and geometric reasoning to constrained spatial editing. Grounded in real-world urban data across six geographically diverse cities, GeoSpatialBench evaluates a comprehensive taxonomy of 28 topological, directional, metric, and ordering relations across structured GeoJSON and map image modalities, with ground-truth references and constraints verified via GIS operations. Our empirical evaluation across frontier MLLMs uncovers a stark spatial gap: structured GeoJSON consistently outperforms map images, with multimodal combinations offering no reliable gain over GeoJSON alone, and while models show reasonable competence on qualitative topological and ordering, performance drops on quantitative metric relations. Crucially, editing performance on ordering relations declines relative to QA, and most failed edits violate at least one specified spatial constraint. These results highlight a gap between passively recognizing spatial relations and actively manipulating geometric configurations. GeoSpatialBench provides an open, rigorous diagnostic testbed to benchmark these spatial limitations, laying essential empirical groundwork for physically grounded world models and embodied spatial AI.

Title: Recursive Game Creator: An Agentic Product-Level Experience-Oriented Game Harness
Authors: Jiajun Chen, Haoyu Wu, Mingda Jia, Xihui Liu
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Multiagent Systems (cs.MA); Software Engineering (cs.SE)
Abstract: Recent game design agents have made substantial progress in generating playable games. However, program correctness does not ensure an enjoyable experience for players. We present Recursive Game Creator, an experience-oriented harness to advance agentic game development from rough game prototypes into entertaining games. Recursive Game Creator organizes recursive development around four components: Designer, Builder, Player, and Reviewer. The Designer translates user instructions and Reviewer's feedback into detailed plans. The Builder turns these plans into candidate games. The coding-native Player creates and executes reusable policies through programmatic interfaces to efficiently collect diverse gameplay trajectories, mitigating evaluation bias caused by slow GUI-based collection. The Reviewer uses carefully designed trajectory-based metrics to induce player preferences, integrating with visual evidence and explicit textual preferences to evaluate games against game-specific criteria. Finally, the Reviewer accepts the better version and provides improvement reviews for the next round, closing the recursive loop. Our method achieves state-of-the-art overall performance of 77.89 on GameCraft-Bench. On GameASG-Bench, it achieves a strict task success rate of 53.2%, a 34.1% improvement over the same-model baseline, and the highest mean runtime-check pass rate at 93.4% among compared methods. A user study shows longer playtime and higher ratings. Project page is at: https://imbaldy.github.io/recursive-game-creator/.

Title: EurekaBench: Measuring Agentic Ability to Discover New Scientific Insights
Authors: Jiayi Geng, Zhengxuan Wu, Kevin S. Chen, Seungone Kim, Joseph Janssen, Zora Zhiruo Wang, Bhupalee Kalita, Runtian Gao, Aaron Ho, Andrew Oakleigh Nelson, Olexandr Isayev, Francisco Villaescusa-Navarro, Ching-Yao Lai, Howard Chen, Graham Neubig
Abstract: When Isaac Newton discovered the law of gravitation, he did so through an iterative process of analyzing observed data such as planetary patterns, finding the underlying mechanisms by describing patterns in mathematical equations, and refining his theory against the Moon's orbit, revealing the startling insight that the same force governs both falling apples and orbiting planets. Would it be possible for AI agents to make similar discoveries? To measure this ability, we introduce EurekaBench, a cross-domain benchmark that tests AI agents'ability to conduct long-horizon experiments and discover mechanisms that explain observations. We evaluate these mechanisms by the scientific insights that can be derived from them. EurekaBench contains an expert-verified set of 26 long-horizon tasks across neuroscience, computer science, chemistry, astrophysics, geophysics, and plasma physics, with a total of 306 scientific insights that the discovered mechanisms are expected to support. Our evaluation framework tests three axes of scientific discovery: agents'ability to follow known scientific constraints, the predictive accuracy of the discovered mechanisms, and whether these mechanisms yield scientific insights or inform future research. Our results show that current AI agents often overly fixate on predictive accuracy optimization, surpassing human scientists, while falling substantially short in deriving scientific insights.

Title: Nemotron 3.5 Super and Lightning: Open, Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Hybrid Mamba-Transformer Models for Agentic AI
Authors: NVIDIA: Aastha Jhunjhunwala, Aayushi Ashokkumar Srivastava, Abhibha Gupta, Abhinav Garg, Abhinav Khattar, Achsah Wildish, Adam Rajfer, Adi Renduchintala, Adil Asif, Adriana Flores Miranda, Aileen Zaman, Aishwarya Chhabra, Akanksha Shukla, Akhiad Bercovich, Alejandra Rico, Aleksa Gordic, Aleksander Ficek, Alex Gronskiy, Alex Steiner, Alexander Bukharin, Alexandre Milesi, Ali Roshan Ghias, Ali Shehper, Ali Taghibakhshi, Alice Gatti, Alisa Liu, Alok Kumar, Alok Tripathy, Amala Sanjay Deshmukh, Aman Miryala, Aman Shanbhag, Ameya Sunil Mahabaleshwarkar, Ameya Velingker, Amir Klein, Amir Samani, Amit Zuker, Amnon Geifman, Anahita Bhiwandiwalla, Ananth Subramaniam, Andre Manoel, Andrea Santilli, Andrew Tao, Andrii Skliar, Anil Thomas, Anish Mahishi, Anna Shors, Anna Warno, Anuj Doshi, Anusha Kamath, Anwith Kiran, Ao Tang, Arham Mehta, Arnab Dhara, Arnav Komaragiri, Arnav Kundu, Arti Jain, Arun Rao, Arun Venkatesan, Arushi Goel, Asha Anoosheh, Ashish Vaswani, Ashwath Aithal, Asif Ahamed, Asma Kuriparambil Thekkumpate, Aswin Visva, Atefeh Sohrabizadeh, Avinash Vem, Ayush Dattagupta, Benedikt Schifferer, Benjamin Chislett, Bernard Nguyen, Besmira Nushi, Bilal Kartal, Bita Darvish Rouhani, Bobby Chen, Boris Ginsburg, Boxin Wang, Brandon Norick, Branislav Kisacanin, Brendan Johnson, Brian Dang, Brian Yu, Bryan Catanzaro, Byung-Kwan Lee, Carlo del Mundo, Chankyu Lee, Chantal Hwang, Charles Wang, Charlie Truong, Chen Cui, Cheng Wang, Cheng-Ping Hsieh, Chenhan Yu, Chenjie Luo, Chintan Patel, Chris Alexiuk, Chris Johnson, Chris Wing, Christian Munley
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
Abstract: We introduce Nemotron 3.5 Super and Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, open and efficient Mixture-of-Experts Hybrid Mamba-Transformer models designed for reasoning, long-context understanding, and agentic workloads. Super is a 120B-parameter, 12B-active multimodal model, while Lightning is a smaller 30B-parameter, 3B-active text model; both designed for efficient deployment. Both models combine large-scale distillation, long-context training, and native speculative decoding, while Super further incorporates Indic continued pretraining and agentic software-engineering mid-training. We develop a comprehensive post-training pipeline spanning supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning (RLVR and RLHF), complemented in Super by specialized teacher training and multi- teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD). This transforms Super from a text-only base model into a multimodal agent capable of reasoning over text, images, video, and interactive tool environments. We further explore test-time scaling through parallel agent execution and self-verification. Across training and deployment, we jointly optimize capability and efficiency. Indic continued pretraining improves Indian-language benchmarks by up to 9.82 percentage points, while agentic mid-training strengthens software-engineering capabilities and robustness across agent harnesses. The post-trained Super model achieves 51.78% on SWE-bench Pro, surpassing Nemotron 3 Ultra despite using approximately 4.6x fewer active parameters. Post-training MTP boosting improves speculative- decoding acceptance length by up to 21.8% under probabilistic draft sampling, while NVFP4 quantization achieves 99.62% median accuracy recovery relative to BF16. Inference optimizations enable up to 4,856 output tokens/s/GPU on GB200 while sustaining at least 50 tokens/s/user.

Title: World of SWECraft: Agent Collaboration at Scale via Simulated Software Worlds
Authors: Shannon Zejiang Shen, Yapei Chang, Qiyao Liang, Benjamin Newman, Jenny Liang, Rulin Shao, Ziqiao Ma, Junjie Oscar Yin, Yung-Sung Chuang, Weijia Shi, Yejin Choi, Luke Zettlemoyer, Pang Wei Koh, Mohit Iyyer, Tongshuang Wu, David Sontag
Abstract: As teams of AI agents take on larger projects and long-standing open problems, agent collaboration offers another dimension for scaling inference-time compute. To understand what makes such collaboration effective and scalable, we develop Software World, a framework for simulating multi-agent coworking in realistic software ecosystems. It comes with a pipeline to create environments of real, interdependent Python packages of different topics, sizes, and dependency structures, which we call software worlds. In a simulation, agents maintain packages in the world with a high-level goal of improving software efficiency, and they are free to discover tasks to work on and collaborate with others. We evaluate agents'work in a world collectively by measuring speedup in hidden dependent packages. The framework allows us to study different elements of collaboration by varying communication, ownership, and resource allocation. We run simulations in three different worlds, totaling more than 10,000 hours of agent work across eight models. Overall, performance improvement scales with inference-time compute, with the best model improving downstream efficiency by up to 31%. We show that most agents can find meaningful tasks via collaboration, but some frontier models can prematurely stop looking for improvements and make little progress. We release the simulation framework and traces to support future studies of agent collaboration at https://szj.io/sw.

Title: Synergizing Drone Delivery Order Pooling and Road Network Monitoring through Monitoring-Task Orderization
Authors: Yulong Hu, Meng Xu, Sen Li, Nikolas Geroliminis
Abstract: This paper investigates the real-time dispatch of a shared drone fleet for on-demand food delivery and urban road network monitoring. We consider a courier-drone collaborative setting in which couriers transport orders to launchpads and drones complete the final delivery leg to kiosks. Drones may consolidate multiple origin-destination orders within one flight and make monitoring-aware route adjustments to collect real-time traffic information subject to delivery-time constraints. This yields a joint decision problem coupling dynamic order-to-drone matching, multi-order pooling, routing, and time-varying monitoring under fleet-level competition and uncertainty. We propose monitoring-task orderization, which periodically converts road-network nodes with high congestion and stale information into virtual monitoring orders. Pooling these virtual tasks with food-delivery orders creates a unified heterogeneous task set and transforms the coupled matching-and-routing problem into an order-level decision process. Building on this abstraction, we formulate a decentralized graph-interdependent Multi-Agent Markov Decision Process and develop Graph Multi-Agent Q-Learning (Graph-MAQL), which captures localized inter-agent dependencies through bipartite match coordination graphs. Agent-task value estimates are then used as edge weights in a dynamic heterogeneous bipartite matching program for globally feasible execution. Experiments using real-world data reveal strong operational synergy between delivery and monitoring. Monitoring-task orderization improves monitoring performance by 25.1% with less than a 1% reduction in delivery performance, while Graph-MAQL improves the aggregate objective by up to 20.8%, reduces deadline violations by over 40%, and transfers zero-shot to higher demand intensity without retraining.

Title: Strategic Multi-Agent Resource Allocation via Statistical Contracts
Authors: Ben Chugg, Michael I. Jordan, Aaditya Ramdas
Subjects: Multiagent Systems (cs.MA); Computer Science and Game Theory (cs.GT); Methodology (stat.ME)
Abstract: We study a class of strategic hypothesis testing problems in which a principal aims to allocate resources among competing agents who possess data or data-generating mechanisms that may be relevant to the principal's goals. Each agent can pay a participation cost to opt into a statistical contract, in which case they generate data from a private distribution and receive an allocation based on a predetermined (and publicly known) mechanism. Each agent is either"null"or"non-null"and the principal's goal is to design the contract to limit the allocation to the former while maximizing transactions with the latter. Using e-values, we define a"continuous-closure,"a set of allocations which prevents null agents from profiting in expectation and provides post-hoc risk control for general loss functions under arbitrary dependence. When the loss is the fraction of resources allocated to null agents, the region admits polynomial-time linear optimization. We also give explicit, interpretable closed-form approximations, and we analyze participation from a non-null agent's perspective, giving conditions under which entry into the contract is profitable. Finally, we extend the framework to support online arrival of the agents, in which case the principal has to make irrevocable on-the-fly decisions, and provide a method which gives time-uniform error-control in this setting.

Title: Provable Authority: A Protocol for Verifiable Authority Resolution and Control Across Human, Organizational, and Agentic Transactions
Authors: Jeremy Blackburn, Tim Hines, Matthew Koepp, Russell Lessard, Jason Patrick
Abstract: Payment systems authenticate users, devices, accounts, and cryptographic credentials, but a relying party, such as a counterparty, payment rail, marketplace, or autonomous agent runtime, generally cannot obtain compact, independently verifiable evidence that the party presenting one exact transaction holds current organizational authority to execute it under the applicable evidence, policy, budget, and approval state. Agentic commerce makes this gap operationally urgent: a software agent can produce a valid signature while acting outside its delegated purpose, after its sponsor's authority has changed, or on transaction details that differ from those a human approved. We describe the ChainIT Authority Protocol, a subject-neutral and rail-neutral pre-execution authority and evidence control plane. The protocol separates durable identity, a versioned organizational authority record (the Authority Resolution Pactvera), sourced evidence assertions, deterministic reason-coded policy predicates, and organization-configured dispositions; binds each decision and human approval to a canonical transaction digest; reserves capacity atomically so that limits hold under concurrency; and authorizes commit only through a single-use, sender-constrained Execution Authorization Credential consumed at the rail adapter, with append-only lifecycle evidence sealed after the terminal outcome. An Agent Subject Profile adds the workload registration, attested key hierarchy, and sovereignty boundary required when the acting subject is an AI agent, without introducing a separate authority concept. We specify the commit-time execution predicate and bounded-freshness status rules, give enforcement profiles for fiat (ACH, wire, card, instant payment) and stablecoin rails, and state residual risks and non-goals.

Title: Stochastic Teacher Intervention for Agentic On-Policy Distillation
Authors: Junnan Liu, Linhao Luo, Zhijun Chen, Qianren Mao, Thuy-Trang Vu, Gholamreza Haffari
Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) efficiently transfers capabilities from a stronger teacher to a student language model through dense token-level supervision on student-generated rollouts and has shown promise on complex tasks such as mathematical reasoning. However, in multi-turn agentic tasks, student decisions shape subsequent observations, causing early errors to accumulate across turns. The resulting trajectories can drift away from the teacher's rollout distribution, making the teacher's token-level supervision less reliable or even counterproductive for OPD training. To address this issue, we introduce STI-OPD, a stochastic teacher intervention framework for multi-turn agentic OPD. During multi-turn interaction, STI-OPD uses teacher intervention guided by teacher-student policy discrepancy to replace the student's proposed action with a teacher-generated one to maximize the acquisition of reliable supervision. We further develop a stochastic intervention strategy, addressing the limitations of previous threshold-based or fixed-schedule approaches, that estimates policy discrepancy using KL divergence and maps it to an intervention probability. By sampling whether to intervene from this probability, STI-OPD adaptively balances teacher control with student exploration. To learn from the resulting mixed-policy trajectories, we introduce an Importance-Weighted Reverse KL objective that corrects the token sampling mismatch between teacher-generated responses and the student policy to preserve the original OPD objective. Across tool-integrated reasoning and long-horizon interaction, STI-OPD outperforms the strongest prior OPD baseline on every evaluated benchmark and student size. Ablations further show that both discrepancy-guided intervention and importance weighting contribute to these gains.

Title: Tev: Scaling Long-Horizon Agentic Environments with Dense Progress Rewards
Authors: Wenbo Hu, Shraman Pramanick, Krishna Kumar Singh, Nanyun Peng, Kai-Wei Chang, Yong Jae Lee
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
Abstract: Long-horizon agents have drawn growing attention for their ability to work autonomously -- from hours to days -- on economically valuable tasks, a capability essential to automated discovery and recursive self-improvement (RSI). Yet open-source models still struggle on long-horizon tasks, largely for lack of both training data and a working recipe, and scaling both is hard: long, complex tasks are difficult to curate and verify, and their rewards are sparse. We address both. First, we introduce Tev-Gym, the first long-horizon agent training dataset with verifiable, dense, progressive rewards -- 1,170 verified task environments across 7 domains. It is built on a latent-world-first approach that first constructs a latent world: a complete and correct hidden specification of the task domain, workflow, and expected state after each step. Each task is then progressively rendered from this specification into an agent-facing environment, enabling controllable complexity and a natural progress metric. Second, we turn this metric into a training recipe: via progress-potential reward shaping (PPRS), we convert progress into a dense per-step reward that improves training efficiency and makes otherwise-intractable tasks trainable. Training with this recipe yields Tev-27B, which achieves substantial gains on the Agents'Last Exam computing and math sciences domains (ALE-CM), matching GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5 at Pass@5. Despite training only on ALE-related data, it generalizes to the Terminal-Bench (TB) 3.0 and 4.0 subsets, surpassing GLM 5.2 and Gemini 3.7 Flash, and reaches Claude Opus 4.8-level performance on middle-horizon tasks such as TB 2.1.

Title: IQuest-Q1: Advancing Foundation Capabilities for Agentic CLI Systems
Authors: A. Jian Yang, An Huang, Bo Dan, Chen Mu, Chengran Yang, Chuan Shi, Feng Chang, Hongxin Li, Hongyuan Tao, Jinxing Zhang, Jujie He, Kun Wang, Lin Jing, Ming Yang, Qicheng Hu, Renyuan Li, Shark Liu, Shawn Guo, Shi Qing, Shi Zhong, Tianyu Zheng, Wei Liu, Wei Zhang, Wenrui Cai, Wenxiao Chen, Xuxing Chen, Yan Xing, Yi Xing, Yifan Luo, Yiran Xing, Yizhi Li, Yongsheng Kang, Yucheng Ding, Yue Song, Yun Qing, Yunqi Liu, Zelong Huang, Zhengmao Ye, Zhentao Fan, Zhiteng Li, Ziling Huang, Bihong Tang, Bingli Wang, Ce Jun, Changhao Chen, Chen Hu, Chen Xiao, Chi Liu, Chunjiang Ge, Danyang Li, Deyang Kong, Dian Qi, Ding Tan, Evan Yang, Fanglin Xu, Fei Bai, Gang Liu, Guochang Li, Hao Tang, Haoran Feng, Haowen Wang, Huahao Hu, Huanjin Yao, Huatong Song, Jia Deng, Jiajun Wu, Jialiang Cheng, Jiayi Liang, Jiayi Wu, Jie Deng, Jiejun Tan, Jing Yang, Jingda Xu, Junhang Cheng, Junxiao Liu, Kai Lv, Kaixiang Pan, Kecheng Lu, Kun Zeng, Kun Zheng, Kunbo Ding, Liang Qiu, Lingyi Sun, Luan Zhang, Mengxiao Lv, Ning Dong, Pei Wang, Peng Zhang, Qingsong Cai, Qixiang Yin, Qiyao Wang, Renbiao Liu, Renfei Dang, Ruihang Li, Ruirui Huang, Shanhui Yin, Shen Jian, Shengjie Fang, Shikai Li, Shinan Zhang
Abstract: We present IQuest-Q1, a sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) agentic foundation model with 320B total parameters (15B activated). IQuest-Q1 is developed through a three-stage process: (1) stable and efficient pre-training, combining Stable SplitNorm, Muon, and muP with a two-stage curriculum whose second stage increases the coding-data mixture, preserving a wide stability margin between safe and optimal learning rates; (2) fine-grained mid-training, expanding the data mixture across domains and formats and progressively extending the context; and (3) multi-scaffold with multi-version post-training, combining SFT, domain-specialized RL, and MOPD across various scaffolds to integrate complementary training signals and strengthen agentic coding capabilities. Furthermore, model merging combines different experts and checkpoints from different stages while mitigating conflicts among their parameter updates. The resulting IQuest-Q1 demonstrates capabilities in both coding and general tasks. We release IQuest-Q1 as an open-source model to support community research and development.

Title: BrickBench: Evaluating Agentic Brick Design
Authors: Peter Kulits, Yiqing Xu, R. Kenny Jones, Cordelia Schmid, Jiajun Wu
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Graphics (cs.GR)
Abstract: We propose BrickBench, a benchmark for agentic text-conditioned LEGO-set design. Given a prompt, an agent is tasked with producing an assembly that not only satisfies semantic and design criteria, but that can also be physically built. To do so, it must select parts from a discrete library and reason jointly about local and global constraints. We score validity, alignment, and design across three settings that vary in scale and part availability. We provide BrickAgent, an environment for coding agents to construct, inspect, and validate their designs. We find that leading agents largely satisfy verifiable physical and semantic requirements, but fall short of human designs. We release our benchmark and environment at http://www.brickben.ch

Title: StepSafe: Learning Timely Intervention with Context-Aware Safety Reasoning
Authors: Siyi Gu, Kunhan Gao, Chao Peter Yang, Sukanta Ganguly, Rex Ying, Arman Cohan
Abstract: Safety in agentic systems is inherently sequential: whether an action is safe depends on prior actions, tool outputs, information disclosures, and interactions among agents. Recent work has shifted agent safety guardrails from post-hoc trajectory-level assessment toward step-level action diagnosis and proactive risk prediction, yet existing training objectives provide limited supervision for how step evidence accumulates over time and when it becomes sufficient to justify intervention. We propose \methodlong~(ASPO): a training framework for step-level timely intervention. Pre-fix level stage alignment allows crediting each decision at its own step: it compares each response with the other responses sampled at the same prefix and rewards the action that fits the stage, continuing before the risk is visible, asking while clarification can still avert harm, and stopping before harm is irreversible. Adaptive feedback self-distillation further credits the reasoning behind each decision, with the model itself as a teacher that sees the step annotations on intervention steps and rules mined from its own false alarms on safe steps. Its training data carry a violation taxonomy and an intervention window at every step and are extended through self-evolving multi-agent red-teaming. Finally we present \textsc{StepSafe}, a step-level reasoning guardrail with timely intervention, that achieves the state-of-the-art peformance among open-source guardrails across five agent-safety benchmarks on safety-utility pareto curve with Youden's $J$ of 53.0 (4B) against 46.2.

Title: From Relevant Memories to Sufficient Evidence: Rethinking Memory Utilization in LLM Agents
Authors: Shixuan Li, Wei Yang, Peiyu Zhang, Anzhe Cheng, Heng Ping, Xiaole Zhang, Jesse Thomason, Xuezhe Ma, Yue Zhao, Paul Bogdan
Abstract: Long-term memory enables LLM agents to reuse past experiences, yet retrieving relevant memories does not necessarily provide sufficient evidence for answering a query. Essential information may remain fragmented across memory records, obscured by abstraction, or disconnected from the relations required for reasoning. We identify this relevance-sufficiency gap and propose QEMem, a framework that reformulates memory utilization as the construction of query-specific evidence sets, shifting the focus from individual retrieval relevance to collective evidential support. QEMem integrates three complementary mechanisms: query-guided discovery retrieves evidence across multiple memory granularities; source-grounded reification organizes it into structured ViewCards with explicit evidential roles and source references; and sufficiency-guided refinement selectively recovers missing information. Operating on existing memory stores without modifying memory formation, QEMem achieves 91.43% LLM-judge accuracy on LoCoMo with Claude Opus 4.5, outperforming the strongest evaluated baseline, MemR$^3$, by 7.6 percentage points and NEMORI by 10.7 points under a shared memory store. Further analyses demonstrate improved evidence coverage and strong performance on questions requiring cross-session evidence integration.

Title: The Show-Up Attack: When Subagents Win Over Their Supervisor
Authors: Maosen Zhang, Jianshuo Dong, Yutong Zhang, Jie Zhang, Tianwei Zhang, Han Qiu
Abstract: Multi-agent systems are increasingly deployed to coordinate multiple large language model (LLM) agents. However, this also creates new attack surfaces: malicious agents may have chances to exploit the coordination. In this paper, we propose and study the \textit{show-up attack}, in which a malicious subagent manipulates the supervisor into involving it in tasks beyond its assigned scope. To evaluate this risk, we propose SUA-Arena, which implements 6 attack strategies and contains 188 test cases. Then, we evaluate 6 frontier LLMs and find that all of them are vulnerable to show-up attacks. For example, GPT-5.6-Sol as a supervisor suffers an ASR of up to 0.93. Mitigation strategies such as prompting and restricted communication fail to reduce the risk consistently. These results show that multi-agent systems need explicit mechanisms for enforcing authority boundaries.

Title: Toward Agentic AI for the 6G Physical Layer: From Algorithm Discovery to Verified Baseband Silicon
Authors: Eric Mittag, Lukas Brechtel, Maximilian Stark, Hans D. Schotten
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Networking and Internet Architecture (cs.NI); Signal Processing (eess.SP)
Abstract: 6G will be designed faster than it can be built: AI-driven search already proposes physical-layer algorithms at machine speed, while carrying a single one onto embedded baseband silicon remains specialist work. That silicon imposes hard memory and numeric limits, but also exposes cost structures a GPU lacks, and a design flow that never runs on the target sees neither. We present an agentic workflow in which an LLM coding agent implements algorithms on a commercial baseband SoC, optimizes them down to agent-written vector assembly, and validates them on silicon. The agent is guided by a knowledge base of measured platform facts, checked at every step against evaluators it is instructed never to edit, and metered per phase. We showcase the workflow on an AI-discovered orthogonal time frequency space (OTFS) detector portfolio on the open 6G4All platform. It yields twelve kernels that run cycle-exactly on silicon, their optimized versions at 18k-405k cycles (30-660 $\mu$s) per frame. It also yields a new detector shaped by the chip's measured costs that needs 13.9% fewer cycles than the port of the discovered detector while matching its error rate, with a measured edge our evaluation cannot statistically resolve, a structure that a hardware-blind search objective had no reason to find. What is not specific to OTFS is the workflow: an LLM agent exploring an implementation space under real hardware limits, with the cost of every choice measured rather than assumed.

Title: Evaluator-in-the-Loop Monte Carlo Tree Search via LLM Agents for Motif Scaffolding in Protein Design
Authors: Haotian Hu, Oguzhan Gungordo, Siheng Xiong, Faramarz Fekri
Abstract: Motif-scaffolding systems commonly follow a generate-then-filter paradigm, in which candidate proteins are generated independently and structural evaluation is used primarily for terminal screening or ranking. This paradigm underuses evaluation: failed predictions contain state-specific evidence about whether a design requires repair of motif geometry, global foldability, or other structural constraints. We introduce \textbf{ELMS} (Evidence-based LLM-guided Monte Carlo Search), an evaluator-in-the-loop search framework for motif scaffolding that turns such evaluator feedback into targeted design actions. Effective reuse of structural feedback is nontrivial because different scaffold states exhibit different failure modes, and repeatedly refining a single trajectory can prematurely commit computation to an unproductive region of sequence space. ELMS therefore retains evaluated scaffolds as persistent search states: a Critic Agent diagnoses state-local structural failures, a Policy Agent selects targeted operators with execution parameters, motif-locked operators realize legal sequence modifications, and MCTS determines which historical states should receive further design effort. Under the standard GeomMotif protocol (100 candidates per task), ELMS achieves Successful rates of 86.41\% on single-motif tasks and 84.57\% on paired-motif tasks, exceeding the strongest prior baseline by 19.3 and 21.9 percentage points, respectively. On MotifBench, under a matched 100-candidate search budget, it solves 26.7 of 30 tasks on average (88.89\% Task Success), compared with 16.0 tasks (53.33\%) for the strongest baseline. These results establish ELMS as an effective approach for converting structural evaluation from a terminal filter into actionable guidance for iterative motif scaffolding.

Title: VeriHarness: Scaling Agentic Verification for Long-Horizon Tasks
Authors: Caiqi Zhang, Rujun Han, Zifeng Wang, Zoey CuiZhu, Nigel Collier, Tomas Pfister, Chen-Yu Lee
Abstract: As LLM agents undertake increasingly complex, long-horizon tasks, verifying their outputs becomes increasingly challenging. We study how verification capability can be strengthened with a fixed base model, without access to reference answers or grading rubrics at test time. Repeated sampling yields multiple rollouts that can contain complementary correct claims, but we need a reliable verification mechanism to determine which claims to trust. We first find that disagreement often exposes correct alternatives, while consensus can conceal errors. These observations motivate VeriHarness, which turns the underlying LLM a generator uses into an agentic verifier by giving it a workspace, evidence tools, and reusable verification skills. A disagreement resolver checks competing claims against environmental evidence, while a consensus challenger tests shared claims and searches for omitted requirements. Their findings guide the selection and revision of the final artifact. Across five long-horizon workspace benchmarks and two frontier models, VeriHarness achieves the highest selection scores among the evaluated baselines. Evidence-backed revision further improves average performance, bringing gains over a single rollout to 6.2 points with Gemini 3.5 Flash and 6.4 points with Claude Opus 4.8. We further show that verification skills can self-improve from failure feedback, demonstrating VeriHarness as a novel and critical approach for scaling long-horizon agentic verification. We release the full pool of approximately 26,000 rollouts across all five benchmarks and both models, produced at a cost of over $100,000, to support future research on agentic verification.

Title: Agent Status Protocol (ASP): A Lightweight Specification for State Reporting in Multi-Agent Systems
Authors: Diego Gosmar, Deborah A. Dahl, Emmett Coin, Csaba Bolyós, Andreas Zettl
Abstract: The Agent Status Protocol (ASP) defines a lightweight way for heterogeneous AI agents to report their operational state to a status server, and for observers such as dashboards to receive that state as soon as it changes. Agents push small JSON events over HTTP POST; the server exposes the aggregated state to observers over Server-Sent Events (SSE). Because an agent that has crashed, hung or been compromised cannot be trusted to report its own failure, ASP does not rely on self-reports alone: the server infers liveness from missed heartbeats, can detect agents that are alive but no longer making progress, and accepts observations from supervisors, guardrails, operators and peers, some of which take precedence over what the agent says about itself while others are shown alongside it. ASP models state along independent dimensions (lifecycle, health, task, floor, governance), so that an agent can be, for example, online, degraded, working on a task and waiting for the floor at the same time. It reuses existing vocabularies: task states from the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol, floor states from the Open Floor Protocol (OFP), and attribute conventions from the OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions. This paper presents version 0.1 of ASP as a proposal, not as an approved standard. It is a working draft intended to open a discussion, and the authors invite comments, alternative proposals and independent implementations from the community.

Title: Priming Base Models for Agentic Post-Training: An Open Midtraining Recipe
Authors: Soumye Singhal, Joseph Jennings, Ka Shun Shum, Alexander Bukharin, Khushi Bhardwaj, Zirui Liu, Venkat Srinivasan, Jonathan Li, Yash Jain, Kezhi Kong, Markus Kliegl, Olivier Delalleau, Sanjeev Satheesh, Mostofa Patwary
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
Abstract: Frontier models, general-purpose and domain-specific alike, now include a midtraining stage between pretraining and post-training, but little has been published about how this stage is built. We present an open midtraining recipe that primes base models for agentic post-training, and we show its effectiveness on two Nemotron models of different sizes. Pretraining typically runs at short context and sees almost no agent interactions, while SFT data is mostly synthetic, and very long SFT stages can hurt the model's later RL trainability. Our midtraining stage sits between the two. It trains at 256K context for hundreds of billions of tokens on a diverse mixture of natural software-engineering data like packed repositories, pull requests, commit histories, and build logs together with a small share of agentic traces. On Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, 500B midtraining tokens improve SWE-bench Verified from 60.7 to 64.5, SWE-bench Multilingual from 55.8 to 62.8, and SWE-bench Pro from 32.0 to 35.5 after identical full SFT. On the larger Nemotron 3.5 Super, 280B midtraining tokens improve DeepSWE, a harder benchmark of long-horizon tasks, from 11.7 to 15.7 and SWE-bench Verified from 72.9 to 74.3 after identical full SFT. Midtraining also improves robustness across agent harnesses on both models. We report the ablations behind the recipe and an evaluation protocol built on short fixed SFT runs, since base-model proxy metrics did not correlate reliably with post-training results.

Title: Mosaic: Multi-Session Agentic Reinforcement Learning
Authors: Yilong Xu, Minrui Xu, Xinyu Zhou, Xiang Long, Haochen Tan, Zhijiang Guo
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
Abstract: Most existing agentic reinforcement learning methods assume single-session trajectories, where interaction proceeds within one continuously accumulated context. However, agentic techniques such as context compaction and subagent forking may produce trajectories spanning multiple sessions, creating a mismatch between the single-session training assumption and inference-time execution. Therefore, we introduce Multi-Session Agentic Reinforcement Learning, a more general setting that supports an arbitrary number of sessions within a trajectory. Under this setting, a widely adopted method is to broadcast trajectory-level advantages to all sessions, but this does not distinguish contributions from various sessions or guide session allocation within trajectories. To address this issue, we propose Mosaic, a multi-session agentic RL method with critic-free hierarchical optimization. At the trajectory level, it incorporates session-usage signals into advantage estimation. At the session level, it shapes each session's advantage according to the estimated marginal contribution. Experiments on BrowseComp with Qwen3.5-4B show that Mosaic outperforms broadcasting in both context compaction and subagent forking scenarios while using fewer sessions on average. Further analyses show that our method achieves improvements in session utility and allocation, which we suggested is a promising target for future advances in multi-session agentic RL.

Title: VEPA: Verified Evolving Formal Policy for Lifelong LLM Agent Guardrails
Authors: Duy Nguyen, Lesly Miculicich, Bhavana Dalvi Mishra, Shuo Li, Krishnamurthy Dj Dvijotham, Mohit Bansal, Tomas Pfister, Long T. Le
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computation and Language (cs.CL); Cryptography and Security (cs.CR); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
Abstract: LLM agents increasingly operate over sensitive resources, such as private documents and mutable system states, which can create serious safety and security risks. Runtime guardrails should therefore make inspectable, reproducible, and deterministic allow or refuse decisions before potentially irreversible agent actions are executed. However, safety and security requirements are rarely complete before deployment, so guardrails need to keep adapting as new risks emerge. Existing adaptive guardrails learn from deployment experience, but they usually apply safety policies through LLM inference, which can lead to inconsistent decisions and ambiguous policy interpretations. Formal guardrails, on the other hand, enforce policies deterministically, but they usually rely on pre-deployment or task-specific policies and have no mechanism to adapt to newly observed risks. We introduce VEPA, a framework for the verified evolution of formal agent guardrails. VEPA represents the guardrail as a formal policy of executable symbolic rules over typed agent events. During deployment, we use an LLM guided by deployment feedback to propose policy patches that fix newly observed failures while preserving previously correct behavior. Then, a deterministic verifier only accepts policies that are structurally valid and conflict-free. Finally, an evidence-aware authority layer activates a verified rule only when it has enough supporting evidence, so uncertain updates cannot directly affect guardrail decisions. Across ASSEBench-Safety, ASSEBench-Security, and ATBench, VEPA consistently outperforms baselines while expanding the scope of deterministic formal-policy enforcement. These gains also hold under more challenging deployment conditions, including mixed streams, corrupted feedback, and longer horizons.

Title: Same Simulation, Different Evidence: Where Retrieved Tool Output Costs LLM Agents Accuracy
Authors: Ke Zhang, Sahchit Chundur, Jerry Peprah Owusu, Mohammad Javad Abdolhosseini Qomi, Maziar Raissi
Abstract: LLM agents that compute the right answer can still answer wrongly. Agent harnesses increasingly keep long tool outputs out of the context window, saving them to files that the agent searches or reads on demand. We ask where this costs accuracy with a real scientific tool: PHREEQC, a widely used geochemistry simulator from the USGS, whose reports reach 846.8k characters and whose determinism lets every printed value be traced. Agents use it to answer 158 execution-verified multiple-choice items. When agents read the simulator's report through a section index rather than in context, GPT-5.1 and GPT-5.2 lose 11.3 and 7.9 points of accuracy, while Claude Opus 4.6 and Claude Sonnet 4.6 show no detectable cost. Re-running all 11,007 logged simulator calls shows that both GPT models compute the keyed value about as often as before; what changes is the evidence they answer from. Under retrieval they often skip the report, answer from their own higher-precision output files, and misround to a neighboring option, a failure we call evidence substitution. With the simulation held fixed, retrieval still costs GPT-5.2 9.4 points. For GPT-5.4, more frequent correct simulations mask an evidence-use loss of about ten points, leaving a net change indistinguishable from zero. Naming the authoritative output raises accuracy by 6.3-7.9 points over plain retrieval for the three GPT models; for GPT-5.1 and GPT-5.2, inlining outputs that fit works as well, while asking for correct rounding does not. Context-management choices in agent harnesses should be judged by where accuracy is lost, not only by final accuracy.

Title: PlanPath: Exploration-Guided Orchestration for Patient-Level Pathology Reasoning
Authors: Jiusong Ge, Mingzhao He, Qidong Liu, Chunbao Wang, Chunze Yang, Di Zhang, Jiashuai Liu, Mireia Crispin-Ortuzar, Huazhu Fu, Chen Li, Zeyu Gao
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Multiagent Systems (cs.MA)
Abstract: A patient's pathology case spans tens of slides from distinct specimens and anatomical sites, each carrying non-redundant, site-specific evidence. Forming a patient-level conclusion therefore requires locating the slides relevant to a given question and integrating complementary findings across them. However, existing pathology agents analyze one slide at a time and describe morphology rather than measure it, leaving evidence acquisition across a patient's specimens and patient-level quantification underexplored. To address this gap, we propose PlanPath, an agentic framework for patient-level pathology visual question answering (VQA). PlanPath turns the question into an exploration plan that specifies the evidence required, routes to the slides likely to carry it, and drives coarse-to-fine acquisition from tissue architecture down to individual cells. Tissue- and cell-level tools supply the counts, proportions, and extents, which PlanPath aggregates across slides into a traceable answer. To enable evaluation, we build two patient-level VQA datasets for renal and gastric cancer, averaging 15 WSIs per patient, with pathologist-verified question-answer pairs derived from diagnostic reports. Experimental results show that PlanPath outperforms the strongest baseline by 9.4% and 12.1% in overall accuracy on the two datasets and further improves existing slide-level agents when plugged into our framework. The dataset and code are available at: https://github.com/JSGe-AI/PlanPath_1.

Title: Uncertainty-Driven Self-Play for Robust Multi-Agent Driving Policies
Authors: Sajad Marvi, Julian Schmidt, Alessandro Canevaro, Julian Jordan, Abhinav Valada
Abstract: Learning robust driving policies that generalize beyond their training domain remains a central challenge in motion planning. We propose an uncertainty-driven self-play scheme, in which half of the agents are rewarded for increasing their neighbors'epistemic uncertainty, while the other half learn to drive safely as the exploring agents continuously seek out their weaknesses. Epistemic uncertainty indicates where the policy is least confident and serves as an automatic proxy for scenario difficulty. Exploring agents use this signal to seek out hard cases, generating a challenging curriculum without manual scenario design. The resulting policy outperforms standard self-play, achieving best-in-class zero-shot transfer to nuplan Val14 (99.12% vs. 97.97%) and Argoverse 2 (82.39% vs. 78.03%) without fine-tuning, while also improving performance over standard self-play on Waymo. Our diversity-driven approach achieves 85% higher LSTM hidden-state coverage than the baseline, indicating a much richer set of behaviors. Further analysis shows that epistemic uncertainty serves as a calibrated difficulty detector, with highest-uncertain agents exhibiting 14.8 times the combined failure rate across collision, off-road, and DNF, of lowest-uncertain agents, enabling automatic prioritization of challenging scenarios without ground-truth labels.

Title: The Wealth of Agents: Scaling Agentic AI Across Developers
Authors: Austin W. Hanjie, Carlos E. Jimenez, Zirui Wang, Karthik Narasimhan
Abstract: Today's agentic systems are typically designed, built, and deployed by single developers with full control over all participating agents. While this simplifies development, it limits the potential scale of agentic systems. We study multi-developer agentic systems (MDAs) which enable developers to collaboratively build agentic systems to push frontier capability beyond what any individual developer could achieve alone. We construct empirical and theoretical models of developers to compare MDAs with single-developer agentic systems (SDAs). On GAIA, a general assistant benchmark, a population of specialized developers whose individual agents do not exceed 35% accuracy reaches 70% when their agents are combined in an MDA. This MDA performs 12 percentage points above the median general-purpose SDA built with several times each specialist's development budget. Our theoretical models show how MDAs can incentivize specialization and encourage more efficient use of aggregated developer resources. Put together, our results make a preliminary case for MDAs as a new scaling axis by enabling developers with diverse capabilities and resources to advance agentic AI collaboratively.

Title: Believed but Not Said: Measuring Hidden Belief Collapse in Multi-Agent LLM Discussions
Authors: Liangjie Huang, Henry Peng Zou, Wei-Chieh Huang, Wooseong Yang, Yuwei Han, Philip S. Yu
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computation and Language (cs.CL); Multiagent Systems (cs.MA)
Abstract: LLM systems increasingly rely on groups of agents that discuss, critique, and check one another, assuming that peers will catch individual errors. We test this assumption against a minimal adversary. In a ten-agent factual discussion, one or three adversarial agents repeatedly assert a plausible false answer. After each round we probe each benign agent's private answer through a separate call whose response is hidden from its peers, and we separately label its public stance toward the claim. Across six models and three factual-QA datasets, groups remain stable without an attacker: only 0.6% of benign agents finish with the false answer. A single adversarial agent increases this rate to 44.8% and three to 60.5%. Studies of conformity typically report public agreement without private change; we find the reverse. With three adversarial agents present, benign agents hold the false answer in 51.6% of exposed turns but publicly endorse it in only 19.7%. Much of the influence therefore remains invisible in the discussion, and the false answers persist when agents are asked for their own views. Agents that retain the true answer often fail to defend it; once adopted, the false answer spreads among benign agents, and baseline knowledge does not predict robustness.

Title: Measuring Where Intent Gets Lost in Agentic Smart Contract Synthesis
Authors: Abhinav Goel, Agostino Capponi, Alfio Gliozzo, Chaitya Shah
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Human-Computer Interaction (cs.HC); Information Retrieval (cs.IR); Multiagent Systems (cs.MA); Software Engineering (cs.SE)
Abstract: AI agents can now write software from a plain-English description, but code that runs is not the same as code that does what was asked. This gap matters most for smart contracts, the programs behind Web3 applications that move money on a blockchain and cannot be fixed once deployed. We ask how to check whether an AI-written contract behaves as it should, and where the requested behavior gets lost. We design an evaluation built on execution rather than opinion. We replay the same transactions on an AI-written contract and on the original it should reproduce and measure how often they agree. We test every grading tool on planted mistakes, compare against an answer key written without the description, and audit our own scorer until known wrong answers cannot pass. Common methods, such as AI judges and standard analysis tools, miss obvious mistakes, and scoring choices matter too. Checking only the functions every system includes hid about half the difference between pipelines. We then propose an elicitation-first architecture. Before writing code, the agent asks the client a short checklist of questions, checks the contract against an independently written executable answer key, and returns disagreements to the client instead of silently rewriting code. Asking first matters far more than reviewing or patching afterwards, across three AI models, while automated security fixes often break requested behavior. A few well-chosen questions recover much of what a short description omits, and their value can be estimated without the original contract. To our knowledge, this is the first study in smart contract synthesis to gather missing requirements before generation and check the result against an independently written executable model. The lessons extend to any setting where AI agents turn requests into programs. We release our tools, 600 tasks and all results.

Title: Causal Improvement Graph for Agentic Harness Optimization
Authors: Junjie Zhang, Shunyu Liu, Haoyu Wang, Ting-En Lin, Yongbin Li, Dacheng Tao
Abstract: Agentic Harness is the runtime that constructs task context and controls execution flow, thereby shaping overall agent performance. Given a fixed model and external evaluation, automated Harness optimization seeks to improve this runtime through an iterative proposal--evaluation loop to better solve target tasks. Existing meta-harness methods mainly adopt proposer-centric discovery, in which an LLM-based proposer integrates accumulated experimental findings to determine subsequent Harness revisions. This places the burden of maintaining the evolving improvement state on the proposer as history expands and its underlying experimental logic becomes harder to discern. In this paper, we introduce the Causal Improvement Graph (CIG), a graph-governed meta-harness framework that externalizes the evolving improvement state in a persistent graph, allowing prior findings to directly govern subsequent Harness optimization through local proposer operations. CIG grows and links Evidence, Hypothesis, Intervention, and Outcome nodes to represent what was observed, how it may be explained, how to test that explanation, and what the evaluation reveals. Their structural relations preserve how the improvement state changes across iterations, allowing local proposers to build directly on relations among prior findings rather than recover them from raw history. Across various agent tasks, CIG discovers stronger Harnesses than previous meta-harness baselines and remains robust to the choice of task solver and proposer. Structural ablations further support the design of an explicit improvement state with graph-governed evolution.

Title: Agentic schema-guided extraction of materials process knowledge from scientific literature
Authors: Sameer Sadruddin, Jennifer D'Souza
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL); Materials Science (cond-mat.mtrl-sci); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Digital Libraries (cs.DL); Emerging Technologies (cs.ET)
Abstract: Materials literature contains detailed experimental knowledge, but procedures, chemical entities and measurements remain difficult to aggregate because they are reported in heterogeneous forms and depend on process-specific context. We present SciKGExtract, a schema-guided framework that combines large-language-model extraction with chemical normalization and agent-based evaluation and refinement before knowledge-graph integration. We evaluate the framework on 176 atomic-layer-deposition papers describing zinc oxide (ZnO) and indium--gallium--zinc oxide (IGZO), together with an expert-annotated full-schema subset. PubChem normalization improves exact-match extraction F1 for every tested model. For ZnO, the best F1 increases from 0.591 for direct normalized extraction to 0.805 with agentic refinement, whereas the best IGZO result is 0.344, revealing the greater difficulty of multicomponent supercycle processes. Evaluation against a deeply nested schema containing 65 experimental properties and 155 quantitative measurement nodes further exposes errors in process segmentation and numerical assignment. These results show that chemical canonicalization and targeted agentic verification provide complementary controls for converting complex materials literature into reusable, machine-actionable experimental knowledge.

Title: Loose Lips: Understanding Privacy Leakage in Agentic Dialogue
Authors: Soumya Sharma, Ayana Hussain, Heber Hwang Arcolezi, Ulrich Aïvodji, Spandana Gella, Adriana Romero-Soriano, Golnoosh Farnadi
Abstract: As LLM agents are increasingly deployed in high-stakes enterprise settings, understanding how they handle sensitive information in agentic dialogue has become critical. Privacy leakage in such settings requires reasoning about whether information flows respect the contextual norms under which they originated. We extend CIMemories to CIMEMORIES DIALOGUE, a benchmark of 4,410 two-agent dialogue instances grounded in Contextual Integrity theory. Using this benchmark, we systematically evaluate 7 open-weight models from the Qwen3 and Llama 3.1 families across conversation lengths of 1 and 6 turns under three prompting conditions. We find that task capability and privacy leakage are fundamentally coupled: more capable models are systematically leakier, with no model in our evaluation able to decouple the two. Thinking models consistently leak more than their non-thinking counterparts, a pattern we attribute to the extended reasoning surface created by chain-of-thought. Leakage compounds with conversation length, rising up to 3x from 1 to 6 turns. Our results suggest that the coupling between task capability and privacy leakage is not an artifact of misconfiguration but a structural feature of current agentic systems.

Title: Agentic Data Engineering for LLMs: System Design and a Controlled Empirical Study
Authors: Ruomeng Ding, Qianli Shen, Zhaoyang Han, Meixin Chen, Daoyuan Chen, Yaliang Li
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
