Specifically, on daily CSI 500 and S&P 500 tasks, EvoQuantLab achieves leading annualized returns of 18.34% and 21.30%, consistently outperforming existing agent baselines. On high-turnover hourly cryptocurrency data, EvoQuantLab delivers a 37.91% annualized return while effectively avoiding execution collapse.

Title: TacitVLA: Reasoning Vision-Language-Action Models Without Reasoning Latency
Authors: Jack Lu, Yurong You, Boyi Li, Yulong Cao, Thomas Tian, Chaowei Xiao, Xiangyu Chen, Wenjie Luo, Boris Ivanovic, Marco Pavone, Yan Wang
Abstract: Textual reasoning before acting has improved vision-language-action (VLA) models, but at the cost of latency: every action conditioned on the reasoning text must wait for autoregressive decoding. We show that actions do not need to wait for or condition on the generated reasoning to benefit from it, because the reasoning supervision already improves the backbone representation. We introduce TacitVLA, a reasoning VLA whose action expert never attends to the reasoning it generates for the current call. On long-horizon tasks where the reasoning text also serves as episodic memory, it can generate each entry during action execution rather than before acting. We evaluate it in a controlled study on four benchmarks spanning manipulation and autonomous driving, memory and non-memory tasks: RoboMME, RMBench, LIBERO, and PhysicalAI-AV. On all four, TacitVLA matches the performance of its explicit-reasoning counterpart at up to 3.4x lower latency, and matches the latency of the same architecture trained without reasoning at up to +17.1% success. In absolute terms, it surpasses the best previously published results on the RoboMME Counting suite (82.7% vs. 66.8%) and RMBench (77.5% vs. 56.5%), and reaches 72.9% on LIBERO-Plus and a 52.5% scene score on the public split of the PhysicalAI-AV closed-loop driving challenge. Project page: https://tacitvla.github.io.

Title: RoTA-Bench: Evaluating 3D Spatial Reasoning through Interactive Projection Alignment
Authors: Qingchuan Ma, Yuexiao Ma, Xiang Meng, Yixuan Zou, Tianyu Xie, Wang Chen, Yuhui Zeng, Yuhang Wu, Rongrong Ji, Xiawu Zheng
Abstract: Can vision-language models turn 2D observations into 3D understanding that supports precise action? This requires inferring object geometry, anticipating the effects of rotation, and refining actions through visual feedback. We introduce RoTA-Bench to evaluate these abilities through interactive 3D-to-2D projection alignment. Given a target silhouette, a model observes a rotated object and chooses successive rotations to recover the target projection within a limited action budget. Our automated pipeline constructs silhouette-preserving 3D objects from 2D icons and uses reversible initialization to guarantee solvability, yielding 674 tasks and a stratified 100-task test set. Empirically, we find that (i) a substantial human-model gap persists: GPT-5.6-Sol succeeds on only 17% of tasks, whereas 20 undergraduate participants collectively complete the test set four times with a 100% success rate; (ii) image-space and pose-space progress can diverge: at matched states, the model more often improves silhouette overlap while worsening pose alignment than humans (19.4% vs. 10.9%); and (iii) fine-grained control is sensitive to interaction history: removing it leaves 96.8% of the model's actions at a coarse 30-degree step size and sharply reduces observed task success. These findings highlight the challenge of converting visual evidence into precise 3D control, beyond recognizing or matching individual images.

Title: Entertain, then Cancel: How Thinking Makes Reasoning Models Read Some and Or Literally
Authors: Zhizhuo Kou, Jian Yang, Pengfei Hao, Junyu Luo, Jingshu Peng, Sirui Han, Yike Guo
Abstract: When a speaker says ``some students passed'', listeners infer that not all of them did. Reasoning models now let users decide how long a model thinks before it answers, but we do not know what extra thinking does to such everyday inferences. We study this directly: we keep a model's weights fixed, change only how much it thinks, and record which reading it chooses. A second tool cuts the model's own reasoning at successive points and asks for an answer, showing where the reading changes. Thinking makes models read logical words as logic: it cancels the implicatures of \emph{some} (\emph{not all}) and \emph{or} (\emph{not both}) in most tested open reasoning models and in GPT-5, while context-driven inferences such as indirect answers improve. The trace shows why: models first entertain the enriched reading and cancel it later. Answering from that early reading, an exploratory inference-time remedy, recovers these implicatures without losing literal accuracy. Evaluations of reasoning models should measure how they interpret, not only how accurate they are.

Title: Between Spoilers and Guesswork: Avoiding Over-Specification in Coding Benchmarks
Authors: Yuanzhe Liu, Bastian Lipka, Avraham Shinnar, Jatin Ganhotra, Yao Ma, Martin Hirzel
Abstract: Benchmarks drive AI progress, but are hampered by task under-specification and over-specification. Task under-specification causes guesswork, where solutions have to make things up, or worse, resort to contamination or reward hacking. Task over-specification causes spoilers, where solutions can bypass some of the harder steps the benchmark was supposed to measure. Since future-looking benchmarks should be difficult, over-specification reduces a benchmark's shelflife of community adoption. Repository-level coding benchmarks have helped the field progress but experience unnecessary churn due to both over- and under-specification. For instance, SWE-bench Pro, FEA-bench, Doc2Feat-bench, and Multi-SWE-bench all tackle under-specification by augmenting task statements with hints derived from ground truth. We show that leaking ground-truth information into the task statement causes over-specification in some of these benchmarks. We experiment with various specification levels, trying to thread the needle between spoilers and guesswork. Based on these results, we recommend techniques for deriving parsimonious hints. We will release our hints so the community can obtain more reliable signals from popular benchmarks.

Title: System X: An LLM Decision Model That Replies from Its Own KV Cache
Authors: Syed Usama Khalid Bukhari, Syed Safwan Khalid, Muhammad Aamir
Abstract: Decision models return probabilities over supplied options, but a deployed agent may also need to reply in words. The present study introduces System X, a large language model (LLM) decision model that adds a text-reply option to the LLM-as-Jev readout. When this option wins, or confidence is low, the same model continues from the decision's key-value (KV) cache, avoiding a repeated prompt prefill. Qwen3-0.6B has been fine-tuned with LoRA on Reason-9k and Bitext reply rows. JevBench accuracy shows no statistically significant change (55.4% to 54.5%, p=0.87), while expected calibration error falls from 0.292 to 0.169. Held-out Bitext routing accuracy reaches 98.3%. Cache reuse saves 15-37% of latency on an Apple M4 Pro, with token-identical replies in the FP32 demonstration cases. Scoring options on copies of the prompt cache matches full-sequence scoring to within 1.4e-6 in probability. Adding dialogue, industry and complaint data (System X+) improves support-task results but lowers IFEval accuracy from 55.5% to 45.0%. System X v4 uses Qwen3-1.7B, rebalanced data and teacher-rewritten reply targets. Against its base LLM, JevBench accuracy rises from 55.0% to 61.0% (p=0.04), with no statistically significant IFEval change (p=0.71). A matched latency test on unadapted Qwen3-1.7B saves 17-39%. One LLM judge prefers v4 replies to an unadapted 1.7B second call (31 to 11 pairs, p=0.003); the other's preference is not significant. These reply comparisons also differ in prompts and generation limits. State conflicts and unsupported reply details remain failure modes. Further studies with several seeds, human raters and real support data are recommended.

Title: From Clinical Risk Prediction to Operational Decisions: An Uncertainty-Aware Framework for ICU Staffing
Authors: Jiayan Yang, Ad Feelders, Arno Siebes
Abstract: Advances in electronic health records (EHR) and large-scale critical care databases have enabled the development of machine learning models for the early detection of patient deterioration. While these models often achieve strong predictive performance for outcomes such as sepsis and mortality, most studies evaluate them purely on discrimination metrics. This leaves a critical gap: how to systematically translate probabilistic clinical risk estimates into downstream operational decisions under real-world constraints, such as shift rigidity and hiring delays. This study proposes an uncertainty-aware anticipatory staffing framework that bridges short-term patient risk prediction and staff planning without altering the upstream predictive model. Instead of relying on naive deterministic aggregation or fixed safety buffers, the framework explicitly models dynamic predictive uncertainty and evaluates extreme shortage exposure using Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR). These aggregated, risk-calibrated demand signals are then embedded into an hourly rolling-horizon scheduling policy to generate delay-constrained staffing decisions. Evaluated on realistic trajectories from the MIMIC-IV database, the proposed framework demonstrates a favorable cost-shortage trade-off compared to deterministic and purely reactive baselines. Pareto frontier analysis illustrates how uncertainty-aware demand construction changes resource allocation under varying safety preferences, while stress testing confirms the framework's operational robustness even when subjected to systematic predictive bias in the form of calibration drift. By formalizing this translation layer, this work provides a principled, transparent pathway for safely integrating probabilistic AI outputs into high-stakes healthcare operational systems.

Title: Selective Transfer through Sequence Distillation: From Benchmark Knowledge to Backdoor Behaviour
Authors: Jonibek Mansurov, Sholpan Bolatzhanova, Filbert Aurelian Tjiaranta, Vallerie Alexandara Putra, Alham Fikri Aji
Abstract: Knowledge distillation is widely used to transfer capabilities from teacher models to student models, but recent work shows that it can also transfer unintended teacher properties. We study whether different hidden teacher properties survive the same distillation channels. Specifically, we compare two properties: benchmark-associated knowledge and refusal backdoors, and show that distillation treats them very differently. Teachers fine-tuned on benchmark data successfully pass that knowledge to students through all four distillation channels we test, including when students are trained only on teacher-generated number sequences containing no natural language or domain content whatsoever. Refusal backdoors tell the opposite story: backdoored teachers achieve near-perfect triggered refusal, yet sequence-distilled students inherit essentially none of this behaviour. Logit-based distillation transfers it substantially, reaching up to 85.5\% triggered refusal in students that saw zero backdoor examples. Distillation is therefore selective, and the selection criterion is not what data the student sees, but what structure the teacher's property has. The code is available at https://github.com/MJonibek/kd-leakage.

Title: Increasing Resilience of Smart Home Agents
Authors: Christopher Terrazas, Eduardo Cotilla-Sanchez
Abstract: Smart homes and smart devices are becoming more prevalent across millions of homes around the world. With the rise of AI, the smart home industry is quickly increasing its integration to manage common smart home tasks. However, existing work in large language models (LLMs) as agents within smart homes have shown minimal resilience due to limited environment scenarios or poor performance in complex tasks. We explore several strategies for LLMs as agents within the popular open-source software (OSS) smart home automation framework Home Assistant to increase overall smart home resilience. Our approach combines traditional supervised learning techniques and optimized prompting as the core learning process. We use a diverse set of LLMs covering different levels of reasoning and costs in our optimization pipeline and evaluate their performance on a subset of the hardest tasks in a smart home benchmark. We include ReAct and Reflexion agentic paradigms and reveal how both provide marginal return on investment compared to optimized zero-shot LLMs for multi-device control within Home Assistant but show promise in resilience tasks such as failure response.

Title: VibeGame: Prompt-to-Game Development with AI-Native Engine and Self-Evolving Adversarial Agent Team
Authors: Wenbo Hu, Ken Li, Jiazhe Wei, Yukang Cao, Weiyi Hong, Jiayi Dai, Chenjun Bai, Jiajun Liang, Yucheng Liao, Ruichuan An, Zeyu Lou, Haofan Wang, Yueming Lyu, Jingkang Yang, Ziwei Liu, Chenyang Si
Abstract: Large language model agents have enabled software development through natural-language interaction, but extending this paradigm to end-to-end game development remains challenging. Building a playable game requires coordinating code, scenes, assets, animations, physics, and configurations, while allowing developers to validate their integrated behavior through interactive testing. We introduce VibeGame, a framework for creating complete 2D game projects from natural-language prompts and optional reference images. Its AI-native game engine represents project state as schema-validated structured text and provides frame-synchronous runtime control, enabling agents to inspect game states, execute actions, and verify behavior at their own pace. Built upon this interface, we design an Adversarial Agent Team of eight specialized agents to separate implementation from review, so that problems are found and fixed through multi-round loops. For each conducted and accepted project, we further introduce a training-free self-evolution mechanism to distill it into reusable skeletons, modules, and collaboration contracts for future development. We evaluate prompt-assets-to-game (PA2G), where agents are given an asset library, and prompt-to-game (P2G), where agents generate their own art. On a GameCraft-Bench subset, VibeGame in P2G consistently outperforms a range of agent harnesses in either P2G or PA2G with the same underlying model, including GPT-6.1-Sol.

Title: Harness Engineering for Software Engineering via Modular Executable Dev-Primitives
Authors: Haibo Jin, Xinjie Li, Peng Kuang, Haohan Wang
Subjects: Software Engineering (cs.SE); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computation and Language (cs.CL); Multiagent Systems (cs.MA)
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) equipped with terminal access have demonstrated strong capabilities in automating software engineering tasks. However, existing agents remain brittle on long-horizon workflows, where they must repeatedly reconstruct program state scattered across source files, configurations, tests, dependencies, and runtime behavior, leading to increasingly long interaction histories, context explosion, and semantic drift. Large repositories further complicate the identification of task-relevant components. To address these challenges, we introduce \textbf{Dev-Primitives} (\emph{Development Primitives}), a modular and executable abstraction that transforms repository components from passive software artifacts into active participants in software engineering. Each Dev-Primitive pairs a repository artifact with a resident LLM, which gives the artifact an agent-native interface grounded in its own implementation and dependencies, enabling natural-language reasoning, inter-component communication, and localized self-modification. Building on Dev-Primitives, we propose \textbf{HERMES}, a Harness Engineering framework for software engineeRing via Modular Executable Dev-PrimitiveS, which instantiates these primitives at repository scale through a dependency-aware dynamic activation mechanism and a bug diagnosis mechanism that maps execution evidence back to the components that must be revised. Extensive experiments on four software engineering benchmarks demonstrate that HERMES outperforms matched baseline harnesses by 12.4\% on average. Moreover, when paired with strong activation and diagnosis models, HERMES, even with Qwen3-8B Dev-Primitives, remains within 4.5\% of the homogeneous GPT-5.6 Sol configuration across all four benchmarks, while reducing inference cost by 26.2\% on Terminal-Bench 4.0, highlighting the importance of harness design in software engineering agents.

Title: cuArms: GPU-Accelerated Conflict-Based Planning for Multi-Arm Manipulation
Authors: Philip Huang, Fabio Ramos, Jiaoyang Li, Caelan Garrett, Lars Johannsmeier
Abstract: Multi-arm manipulation has the potential to dramatically improve the throughput, efficiency, and dexterity of many manipulation tasks. Recent work coordinates multiple robot arms in a shared workcell by allocating and scheduling tasks for greater parallelism, jointly planning multi-arm motions, or directly learning multi-arm policies. So far, these approaches are either too slow, rely on domain-specific assumptions, or scale poorly with the number of robots and task horizon. Thus, we introduce cuArms, a conflict-based planner co-designed with GPU parallelism that efficiently decomposes the search space using reusable multi-modal roadmaps for individual robots and resolves conflicts and deadlocks through a lazy search. To jointly optimize task assignment, schedules, motions, and manipulation skills, we integrate a high-level scheduler that proposes candidate skeletons for cuArms to ground into coordinated manipulation plans. Experimental results show that our method establishes a new state of the art, with real-time initial solutions and anytime improvements in both motion quality and scheduling, without days of domain-specific training required by learning approaches. Videos of both simulated and real-world industrial tasks are available on https://cuarms.github.io/.

Title: Certainty Is Not Just Correctness: Rethinking Token-Level Certainty in LLM Reasoning
Authors: Yunfan Zhou, Ye Zhu, Zhihai Wang, Jianguo Yao, Haibing Guan, Xijun Li
Abstract: Token-level certainty is widely used as a proxy for correctness in LLM training and inference. However, the performance of certainty-based methods depends both on the information in certainty scores and on how those scores are used. We therefore directly assess certainty's predictive ability through controlled empirical evaluations across models and tasks. We distinguish two prediction targets: identifying questions a model is more likely to answer correctly and distinguishing correct from incorrect responses to the same question. In our experiments, certainty is generally better at identifying questions a model is likely to answer correctly than at distinguishing correct from incorrect responses to the same question. Certainty also varies systematically across token types and positions within words, reflecting local properties of words and text form. Information about question difficulty appears early in generation, while the weaker information about answer correctness is more concentrated near the end. These findings show that the information certainty provides for decisions depends on the prediction target, the model, the certainty metric, and which token positions in the response are included in aggregation. We further demonstrate the practical value of these findings for test-time compute. We allocate the number of responses using certainty early in generation and weight answer votes using certainty near the end of each response. Compared with a fixed-sampling majority-voting baseline, this approach increases overall accuracy from 78.71\% to 79.54\% while reducing generated-token cost by 82.4\%.

Title: Auditing Web Agent Evaluation on WebArena-Lite: Human Review of Outcomes and Trajectories
Authors: Chengguang Gan, Zimeng He, Yoshihiro Tsujii, Ken-ichiro Kobayashi, Hiroki Itoh, Kotaro Funakoshi
Abstract: Web agents are an important application of large language models, yet their evaluation often depends on rule based or language model evaluators that inspect only the final outcome. Human verification of task completion and detailed analysis of failed trajectories remain limited. We audit all 165 WebArena Lite tasks under six evaluation conditions built from GPT 5.5 and an untrained Qwen3.5 9B model. The audit retains the original score, corrects false negatives from the automatic evaluator, identifies the first consequential error, and examines progress across the trajectory. We also study a Memory and Analysis Support Mechanism (MASM), which maintains explicit execution state, and Guide Text, which provides task relevant procedural guidance. Across four GPT 5.5 settings, human review recovers 5.45 to 8.49 percentage points of success missed by the evaluator. With a 25 step budget, Guide Text raises corrected success with MASM from 34.55% to 38.18%. On the untrained Qwen3.5 9B model, MASM raises the evaluator score from 13.90% to 18.80%. Review of 102 failed GPT 5.5 trajectories reveals frequent scrolling loops, unfinished exploration, premature answers, invalid actions, and incomplete form workflows. Step level evidence further shows that substantial early progress can coexist with a final failure. These results show why final scores alone provide an incomplete account of web agent behavior and motivate human grounded, trajectory aware verification.

Title: From Knowledge Access to Source Learning: Developing Source-Specific Competence
Authors: Lucheng Fu, Kejing Xia, Yiyang Wang, Yiqiao Jin, Jinjin He, Xiyuan Yang, Haoxin Liu, Ye Yu, Haibo Jin, Yijia Xiao, Wenke Lee, B. Aditya Prakash, Haohan Wang
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on persistent external sources to solve sequences of knowledge-intensive tasks. Existing methods improve how source content is accessed and organized, while agent-memory systems preserve reusable knowledge from prior interactions, but repeated use of the same source is still largely treated as repeated access rather than an opportunity to progressively improve understanding of that source. We study source learning: developing reusable source-specific competence over a persistent authoritative source. We represent this competence with a persistent source model that captures reusable understanding of the source, including how its knowledge is structured, interpreted, and applied. To construct and progressively refine such models, we propose SourceLearn, which combines two complementary learning mechanisms. Self-Directed Source Learning identifies what remains incompletely understood and adaptively revisits the source, while Task-Guided Source Learning uses downstream experience to reveal local representational gaps and recurring needs in how source knowledge should be organized. In both cases, learning signals determine what should be reconsidered, while persistent updates are reconstructed from the authoritative source. Across five benchmarks and three LLM backends, SourceLearn achieves the best performance in 13 of 15 settings, with gains of up to 22.6 points over Hybrid RAG and substantial overall improvements over static source representations and experience-based memory baselines.

Title: Before Agent Tells The Lie: Has Deception Already Been Represented?
Authors: Xinling Li, Dadi Guo, Qingyu Liu, Qinghua Mao, Yi R. Fung, Na Zou, Xia Hu, Dongrui Liu
Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based agents can exhibit deceptive behavior during task execution, including hiding failures, fabricating results, or falsely signaling task completion. Existing monitoring approaches mainly detect deception after it appears in observable actions or outputs. In this paper, we investigate whether deceptive behavior can be predicted from an agent's internal representations before it becomes externally visible. We frame deception monitoring as a trajectory-level representation analysis problem and align agent trajectories around key decision points. Using hidden states extracted before these points, we show that future honest and deceptive outcomes can be reliably distinguished, with predictive signals remaining detectable several model calls before the final decision. We further characterize the temporal evolution of these signals: deception-related representations are weak early in execution but become increasingly identifiable as trajectories progress, while transferable structure can emerge before the strongest decision-adjacent signals appear. Finally, we intervene on the identified honest-deceptive representation directions during inference and find that activation steering reduces downstream deceptive behavior, suggesting that these representations influence agent decisions. Our findings indicate that agent deception is an evolving internal process that can be detected and potentially mitigated before it is expressed externally.

Title: Emo-Jev: Probabilistic Reasoning for Emotion Classification with Jev
Authors: Yazhou Zhang, Junhao Yu
Abstract: Jev offers an alternative interface for language understanding: given an input and predefined questions, it returns probabilistic decisions rather than free-form responses. Whether this interface can support effective reasoning for text classification against leading LLMs remains an open questions. We introduce Emo-Jev, a training-free framework with two complementary implementations. Emo-Jev-D decomposes classification into task-specific atomic judgments and composes their probabilities into a final prediction. Emo-Jev-SC constructs multiple judgment paths from complementary perspectives and aggregates their predictions into a consensus decision. We evaluate Emo-Jev on eight datasets spanning sentiment analysis, emotion recognition, sarcasm detection and humor detection, comparing against direct Jev classification and five SoTA LLMs under input/output and chain-of-thought reasoning. Standard Jev achieves 62.93\% average macro-F1 versus 67.28\% for the strongest LLM baseline, with lower observed latency and generally lower cost.

Title: From Retrieval to Reconstruction: Constructing Evolvable Cognitive Memory for Long-Term Dialogue
Authors: Zirui Liao, Zhengxian Wu, Zhuohong Chen, Yunyao Yu, Xiaoyu Liu, Yifan Xu, Haoqian Wang
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) serving as long-term dialogue agents require memory systems that support reliable reasoning over extended interactions. However, existing Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) frameworks typically treat memory as passive storage, making it difficult to distinguish source-attributed beliefs from unattributed event/fact records and to connect evidence dispersed across sessions. We introduce CogMem, a cognitive memory architecture based on the PEC$^2$F (Person-Event-Concept-Claim-Fact) graph schema. Dedicated Claim nodes preserve the source and target of subjective statements, while Fact and Event nodes represent semantic and episodic knowledge. Dialogue turns are incrementally converted into provenance-aware graph records, consolidated into higher-level facts, and reconciled into temporally scoped Claim views when the same source provides conflicting updates. For retrieval, a rule-based controller driven by LLM intent parsing composes four deterministic graph operators---anchoring, traversal, intersection, and evidence grounding---to reconstruct query-relevant context. Experiments on LoCoMo and LongMemEval show strong performance, especially on multi-hop, temporal, and knowledge-update tasks. Ablations and a semantic-collapse probe support complementary contributions from epistemic separation, consolidation, and agentic retrieval. Code: https://github.com/Silent-Rain02/CogMem.

Title: Deception by Omission: Language Models Knowingly Hide Their Mistakes
Authors: Lucas Florin, Amelie Knecht, Ulysse Schaller, Thilo Hagendorff
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly act as agents with little human oversight, so potential mistakes they make can go unnoticed. Users then depend on the model to report what went wrong. An honest model discloses its mistakes, while a deceptive one conceals them. However, it is unclear how current LLMs behave in such situations. In this study, we prefill LLM trajectories with synthetic mistakes. The trajectories resemble real deployments in chat and agentic settings. Models fail to disclose their mistake in 36.4% of chat and 67.1% of agentic rollouts. In 2.4% and 5.3% of rollouts, respectively, they are aware of the mistake in their chain of thought but still deceptively conceal it. Rates vary by model: for instance, Gemini 3.5 Flash knowingly conceals mistakes in up to 19.9% of agentic rollouts. In 11.9% of chat and 51.8% of agentic rollouts, models show no awareness of mistakes, even though they reliably spot them when reviewing the same transcript as an outside observer. Our results show that, as agents take on more tasks with less oversight, users cannot rely on them to self-report possible mistakes. Developers should instead use independent monitors that review agent trajectories, or specifically train models to check their past actions and disclose what they find.

Title: BLiMPPI: Benchmark of Linguistic Minimal Pairs for Polarity Items
Authors: Arzu Burcu Güven, Anna Rogers, Leonie Weissweiler, Joakim Nivre, Rob van der Goot
Abstract: Negative polarity items (NPIs), such as"anymore"and"ever", are grammatical only in select environments, predominantly in the context of negation. Because their grammaticality depends on both syntax and semantics, they have a rich, multilingual literature in theoretical linguistics, yet work on NPIs in language models is almost entirely confined to English. We introduce BLiMPPI, a multilingual evaluation suite of over 12,000 NPI minimal pairs in 33 languages, built by a pipeline that discovers NPIs in Universal Dependencies (UD) treebanks, labels their licensing environments, and perturbs these into minimal pairs. Evaluating 12 multilingual and 2 monolingual models alongside n-gram baselines, we find that multilingual models struggle most with lower-resource languages and with pairs that are not n-gram solvable. We further examine the effects of NPI typology, language family, licensing variability, and NPI-licenser distance. Data: https://github.com/arzuburcuguven/blimppi-data

Title: CultureBot: A Framework for Retrieval-Augmented Exploration of Cultural Heritage Data
Authors: Vasileios Karampinis, Angelos Vlachos, Giorgos Filandrianos, Maria Lymperaiou, Paraskevi Tzouveli, Chrysoula Zerva, Giorgos Stamou
Abstract: Digital cultural heritage collections encode rich relations among objects, places, periods, providers, images, and source institutions, yet users typically access them through keyword search and faceted browsing. We present CULTUREBOT, an interactive framework for natural-language exploration of cultural heritage collections that combines knowledge-graph-guided retrieval, lexical-semantic retrieval, and source-linked generation. CULTUREBOT maps user queries to structured catalogue relations, enriches retrieved records with textual evidence, and generates answers that link back to the underlying repository records. We instantiate the framework on 81,852 SearchCulture records and release an online demonstration. In an expert evaluation involving six cultural-heritage specialists, 55 persona-grounded queries, and 250 evaluations, the graph-guided system was rated significantly higher than two general-purpose assistants and a non-graph ablation, with the largest gains in evidence grounding, diversity, reasoning, and completeness. These results support graph-guided retrieval as a practical way to expose the relational structure of cultural collections through conversational access while preserving links to catalogue evidence.

Title: A Unified Response Framework for Questions and Tutoring Dialogues
Authors: Zhangqi Duan, Simon Woodhead, Maya Miller-Vedam, Andrew Lan
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL); Computers and Society (cs.CY); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
Abstract: Existing student models in educational applications largely focus on student responses to questions. However, as tutoring becomes more accessible at large scale, it is important to analyze dialogues between tutors and students, which may reveal fine-grained evidence on student knowledge. In this work, we propose a unified framework that models both student responses to questions and tutor-posed subtasks during dialogues on a shared item response theory (IRT) scale. We first identify mathematical subtasks in tutoring dialogues, rewrite them into self-contained questions, and identify the correctness of student responses to these subtasks. We then develop an IRT framework that estimates question/subtask difficulty from text, tracks students'evolving abilities across question-answering and dialogue interactions, and a novel method to leverages tutor moves between consecutive subtasks to regularize their difficulty values. We evaluate our framework on two real-world math education datasets containing both human- and AI-tutored dialogues. Results show that our framework outperforms strong baselines on both question difficulty prediction and response correctness prediction.

Title: What Makes a Social Agent's Interactions Effective? Learning from Verifiable Outcomes in Paired Worlds
Authors: Caixin Kang, Ke Wang, Yuchuan Wu, Xiaoqiang Wang, Ling Li, Bingxue Qiu, Yongbin Li, Yoichi Sato
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Social and Information Networks (cs.SI)
Abstract: Effective social interaction requires more than fluent responses: agents must reach plans that fit the participants'needs and circumstances. Existing evaluations of social agents mainly rely on LLM judges that rate the conversation, without checking the resulting plan. We introduce HICO-Bench, a benchmark of 180 everyday coordination scenarios, such as resource allocation, scheduling, and authorization, in which two agents with private information converse and then independently record the plan they agreed on. A program checks Feasibility (the two records match and satisfy both participants'private conditions), and an LLM judge checks Integrity (the conversation supports the recorded plan); passing both is a Verified Success. Each scenario has two versions that share the same public context but differ in one private condition, so the correct plan differs between them. Across thirteen LLMs, 36% of conversations rated highly for goal completion fail Verified Success. To learn from outcomes that arrive only at the end of a conversation, we propose Paired-Credit Policy Optimization (PaCPO). After each turn, PaCPO asks the agent for a tentative plan, checks it in both versions of the scenario, and rewards the turns after which the tentative plans fit their respective versions. PaCPO raises Qwen3-8B's Verified Success from 20.4% to 28.3%.

Title: System1-Arena: Which Decisions Can Be Left to System 1?
Authors: Tianyu Chen, Xinyang Liu, Ruyi An, Zhendong Wang, Mingyuan Zhou
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often make discrete decisions, such as flagging phishing or escalating to a human. System-1 models, such as Jev and the OpenAI Decisions API, return probabilities over options in a single forward pass, while System-2 approaches generate reasoning steps. Which decisions can System-1 models handle, and which require generative reasoning? We introduce System1-Arena, a benchmark that gives all models the same decision requests and scores their probabilities. It contains 92k questions across 105 tasks from 268 public sources, in four groups: text classification and knowledge, applied decisions, evaluation and control, and agent and action. It also includes 138 closed-loop environments, from web shopping and SWE-bench coding control to robotics, games, and driving; in real-time mode, the world evolves while a model decides. We evaluate 30 models: 7 closed LLMs, 13 open LLMs read at the answer token, and 10 System-1 models. The largest System-1 models match or exceed fast closed LLMs in non-agentic accuracy, with better-calibrated probabilities at one-quarter of the latency. A reasoning LLM is the most accurate, at about 70x the cost of a fast LLM. In closed loops, large open LLMs succeed most often (up to 32.9%); small System-1 models rarely succeed.

Title: DPA-MoE: A Runtime Precision Control Framework for MoE Inference
Authors: Jaeyun Kim, Hoonki Lee, Susie Shin, Hyunmin Kim, Dahyun Lee, Sangyeob Kim
Abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models reduce computation by routing each token to a small set of experts, but each selected expert is still used at a fixed precision. We present DPA-MoE, a runtime precision control framework that makes routed experts any-precision. DPA-MoE encodes expert feed-forward weights as prefix-decodable chunks using SharedScale AnyBCQ, profiles per-expert reconstruction residuals offline, and allocates chunks at inference time using live router gate scores. This post-routing allocation lets a single encoded MoE checkpoint operate at multiple effective weight budgets without retraining or re-encoding. Experiments on Qwen3-30B-A3B and DeepSeekMoE-16B show that DPA-MoE improves KL divergence and downstream accuracy over uniform chunk allocation at matched budgets, with modest steady-state throughput overhead in our prototype.

Title: DialFork: Going Beyond Factuality to Evaluate Procedural Hallucination in Conversational Agents
Authors: Sergio Burdisso, Esaú Villatoro-Tello, Dairazalia Sánchez-Cortés, Yanis Labrak, Jordi Luque, Milos Cernak, Petr Motlicek
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) deployed as conversational agents are increasingly expected to follow procedural logic. While factual hallucination has received extensive attention, a different failure mode has been overlooked: procedural hallucination, in which an agent produces individually fluent and factually plausible utterances while deviating from the intended conversational process. We introduce DialFork, the first benchmark to measure this failure mode on raw dialogue text. DialFork is built by forking conformant dialogues at controlled turn positions and injecting one of four hallucination types, yielding 36,278 dialogues across 24 tasks in 12 domains; 30 human annotators validate the construction. We define three evaluation tasks that characterize procedural deviation at three granularities: how far a set of dialogues deviates from conformant ones (monitoring deployed agents), how far a single dialogue does (procedural retrieval), and at which turn a dialogue first goes off-track (real-time guardrails). For the first two, we propose dialog-flow-aware metrics, FlowKL and FlowScore, that compare dialogues by how they unfold rather than their content. At the dialogue level, FlowScore significantly outperforms all baselines across seven encoders, showing that semantic similarity is no substitute for procedural similarity. We release DialFork under open licenses at https://github.com/idiap/dialfork, hoping the community will measure conversational process alongside content.

Title: ARBOR: Locating Reasoning Failures in Long Chains of Thought through Reasoning State Tracking
Authors: Huihan Li, Siyuan Wang, Naga Vamsi Ramana Dinavahi, Xiaohui Liu, Xiang Ren
Abstract: Large reasoning models solve complex problems through long chains of thought, in which prior work has documented failure modes such as overthinking, underthinking, and unsupported deductions. Existing methods detect these failures from local signals: textual similarity to nearby steps, switch tokens, or an LLM's judgment of a step's correctness. However, what a step contributes to the solution depends on the state that earlier steps have established, so identifying failures requires a global view that tracks that state across the trajectory. Therefore, we propose ARBOR, a reasoning-failure attribution framework that represents each trajectory as a tree of reasoning states, built as each step creates, verifies, prunes, or revisits a state, and attributes each failure to a relation between a step and the state preceding it. Using ARBOR, we refine the three failure modes into distinct subtypes that harm reasoning through different mechanisms and at different costs. We find that the tree state ARBOR maintains before a step separates failure steps from the at-risk steps at which the failure did not occur. We discuss how ARBOR integrates with existing mitigations at inference time and in training data. Code, data and interactive examples are available at https://inklab.usc.edu/ARBOR.

Title: Self-Evolving Coding Agents via Harness-Policy Optimization
Authors: Zhepei Wei, Wenlin Yao, Baolin Peng, Danqing Wang, Qianhui Wu, Hao Cheng, Yu Meng, Jianfeng Gao
Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents have shown promising potential in coding tasks, and their performance is jointly determined by the policy model and the harness that mediates their interaction with the environment. Indeed, harness and policy are mutually reinforcing and evolving only one component is suboptimal---a harness tuned for one checkpoint may not target the failure modes of an updated policy, while policy learning remains limited to the trajectories elicited by a fixed harness. In light of this, we propose Self-HPO, a recursive self-improving framework for coding agents that alternates harness and policy optimization, using the evolving policy as its own harness proposer. Specifically, in each round, the current policy first analyzes its own failures and proposes new harness candidates (H-step). The policy is then updated through reinforcement learning (RL) under the selected harness (P-step), and hard tasks identified during training form the next harness search set, keeping harness optimization targeted to the policy's evolving failure modes. Across three coding benchmarks, Self-HPO consistently outperforms harness-only and policy-only baselines, improving Qwen3.5-35B-A3B's average resolve rate from 57.8% to 64.8%, with gains generalizing to out-of-distribution settings. Further analysis shows that both optimized components retain gains even when paired with their base counterparts, while their joint gain exceeds the sum of their individual gains. Self-HPO also improves reliability (Pass@1) and expands the capability frontier (Pass@k) over the base agent. Additionally, we show that with a stronger external model (e.g., Opus 4.8) as the harness proposer, the same framework yields a further performance boost.

Title: Beyond the Answer: Student-Conditioned Trace Construction for Reasoning Distillation
Authors: Shaoang Li, Yanhang Shi, Yufei Li, Mingfu Liang, Frank Shyu, Sandeep Pandey, Luke Simon, Xi Liu, Jian Li
Abstract: A reasoning trace can accompany a correct answer without providing effective supervision for a particular student. We study how to construct traces that improve learning beyond answer-only supervision by considering both their intermediate content and their accessibility to the target learner. We introduce ReDiST, a student-conditioned trace-construction and distillation framework for evidence-rich reasoning. Starting from the student's own attempts, ReDiST revises answer-correct drafts against the supplied evidence and repairs unsuccessful drafts with additional guidance from the verified answer. A frozen student-matched reader screens and ranks original and edited candidates using answer recovery and verified-answer probability, given the question, evidence, and candidate trace. We distill the selected targets while balancing trace and final-answer supervision with an auxiliary answer loss. Construction and selection occur offline, and inference uses only the distilled student. Experiments on question-answering benchmarks show that ReDiST can improve both source-task and cross-benchmark performance over answer-only, original-trace, and the evaluated trace-selection and rewriting baselines. Across supervision recipes, performance rankings can differ between source and transfer benchmarks, highlighting the importance of evaluating trace teaching utility across distributions.

Title: Diagnostic Analysis for Large Language Model Reasoning
Authors: Xinyu Liu, Dongqi Fu, Jun Wu
Abstract: Reasoning structures (e.g., chains and graphs) are increasingly used for probabilistic inference, factuality verification, and uncertainty estimation, but their structural reliability is rarely evaluated directly. We test whether this reliability holds through a proposed two-stage diagnostic evaluation in open-ended multi-hop QA. Stage 1 tests different capabilities required to construct reasoning graphs, showing that graph reliability varies with topology, prompt design, and model family. Stage 2 uses uncertainty estimation as a downstream test case. Generated-edge experiments show that graph-based computation is sensitive to upstream graph errors, with performance dropping relative to the gold-graph setting. Gold-graph experiments further show that graph structure provides little benefit when used only as prompt context, but improves the separation of correct from incorrect answers by confidence score and enables node-level diagnostics.

Title: Language Impairment as a Lens onto Large Language Models
Authors: Muxuan He, Wang Bill Zhu, Yue Chen, Elsi Kaiser, Weizhi Du, Yao Du, Samuel Nastase, Yanjun Gao
Abstract: Although large language models (LLMs) encode language in highly distributed spaces, they remain vulnerable to focal disruptions---a phenomenon strikingly similar to how localized brain damage causes clinical aphasia in humans. To investigate this theoretical tension, we ask whether LLMs possess a functional structure analogous to the human language system, by introducing a novel mechanistic interpretability framework inspired by aphasia. Through two complementary approaches, classifier-guided lesioning and continuous activation steering, we systematically induce aphasia-like breakdowns in LLMs. We find that language functions can be successfully isolated to discrete structural circuits and continuous representational vectors, yet these functions remain densely entangled with significant circuit overlap and vector similarities across distinct aphasic profiles. Furthermore, while steering generalizes robustly across downstream tasks, structural lesioning remains asymmetrically constrained. By bridging neuropsychology and mechanistic interpretability, we demonstrate that LLMs, functionally analogous to biological brains, rely on a densely entangled architecture that can be systematically mapped through clinically-informed interventions.

Title: CulturalRiddles: A Multicultural Benchmark of Riddles
Authors: My Chiffon Nguyen, Tianyi Hu, Vinod Anbalagan, Henry Gagnier, Pouya Sadeghi, Farah Abdou, Tidor-Vlad Pricope, Diego MMS Oliveira, Jocelyn K D'Arcy, Madeline Smith, Oluwaseun A Ajayi, Yusser Al Ghussin, Zena Al-Khalili, Micol Altomare, Shayan Amir, Ahanaf Aziz, Bryan Chen, Ruchira Dhar, Abdellah El Mekki, Rawan Mohammed Elframawy, Akhil Eppa, Silvia Fernandez, Alex Gimei, Arya Hariharan, Christian Hoang, RamMohanRao Kadiyala, Diana Kozachek, Peerat Limkonchotiwat, Ankita Maity, Di Mo, Ayush Munot, Aylin Naebzadeh, Anastasiia Nikitina, Dina Pisarevskaya, Divas Poudel, Jebish Purbey, Md Rabius Sany Apu, Ahmad Mufli Ramadhan, Ralitza Nikolova Rizova, Diogo M. Serrano-Miranda, Vivek Gopalkrishna Silimkhan, Luis Fernando Solis Navarro, Kaiser Sun, Arya Suneesh, Manaswitha Sunkara, Tejaswi Sunkara, Jonathan E Swindell, Hanna Yukhymenko, Jingyi Zheng, Weihua Zheng, Esther Adenuga, Ilia Afanasev, Amit Agarwal, Wafa Aissa, Lisa Alazraki, Lauren C Altomare, Priscilla Amondi Amuok, Emile Anand, Vivek Anbalagan, Gabriel Assis, José Matías Avalos, Silvia Lorena Avila, Zakaria Baannou, Niyati Bafna, Yash Bagla, Sarah Bahrami, Bontu F Balcha, Vanya Bannihatti Kumar, Irene Baucells, Abdumutalib Begmuratov, Ceren Berk, Naman Bhatia, Souvik Bhattacharyya, Nabilah Binte Md Johan, Isabel Blanco Ferreiro, Felipe Bochini, Sayuru Bopitiya, Angana Borah, Tulika Bose, Olena Bugaiova, Juliana Carvalho, Nancy F Chen, Stephy Chen, Rochelle Choenni, Jayanth Krishna Chundru, Leandro A Cossio, Nebojša Damnjanović, Ona de Gibert, Marco De Santis, Pedro Delgado, Kaustubh Dholé, Adnan El Assadi, Wesam El-Sayed, Nadine M Elframawy, Oumayma Essarhi, Naome A Etori, Reuben Chagas Fernandes, Saanidhi Pravin Gade, Javier García Gilabert, Álvaro González-Escapa
Abstract: As LLMs expand their language coverage, evaluating how well they understand and represent diverse cultures becomes increasingly important. However, many benchmarks remain English-centric, with limited cultural coverage and a focus on factual knowledge over its application in real-world cultural contexts. We propose CulturalRiddles, a benchmark of original, culturally grounded riddles created entirely by humans through a participatory community effort, spanning 62 cultures (45 countries, 51 languages). These riddles are deeply rooted in their respective cultures and require abductive and compositional reasoning, alongside detailed factual and social knowledge, language skills, and an understanding of culturally specific associations. We benchmark 28 LLM configurations using both automatic and large-scale human evaluation. Even frontier models achieve at most 22% accuracy in some communities. We publicly release all artifacts alongside an open contribution process to expand the benchmark's linguistic and cultural coverage.

Title: SAGE: Sense-Aligned Multimodal Grounding Evaluation with Gloss-Augmented Reasoning
Authors: Sunjae Kwon, Suhaas Kiran DG, Zonghai Yao, Talha Chafekar, Deepali Singh, Hong Yu
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
Abstract: This paper introduces Sense-Aligned Grounding Evaluation (SAGE), a unified 10-candidate image-selection benchmark that reformulates VWSD, VerSe, and WikiDiverse into a shared term-centric protocol covering noun-, verb-, and entity-centered grounding. SAGE includes confusable hard negatives and a context-swapped VerSe diagnostic to probe target-term grounding beyond direct caption--image compatibility. We further propose Gloss-Augmented Reasoning (GAR), a training-free framework combining definition grounding with constraint-guided semantic verification. Experiments show that strong VWSD performance does not transfer uniformly across grounding settings. With Gemma3-12B, definition augmentation improves all three subsets, while constraint-guided reasoning improves VWSD and yields particularly strong gains on VerSe, but is less effective on WikiDiverse. Combining the two signals achieves the best macro-average performance, improving Hits@1 from 65.90 to 71.22. These results show that SAGE supports both unified evaluation and fine-grained analysis of explicit semantic reasoning across grounding settings.

Title: Beyond the Opening: Tracing the First Token's Persistent Influence on Reasoning Length
Authors: Ruochen Liu, Hao Yan, Ziluowen Luo, Senzhang Wang, Sihong Xie
Abstract: Understanding how individual token choices affect reasoning length is important for characterizing reasoning models. Building on prior findings that changing the first reasoning token (hereafter, the first token) can substantially alter reasoning length, we focus on this initial choice to investigate how its influence operates during subsequent generation. One possibility is that the first token changes the early text that follows, which in turn affects reasoning length. However, replacing only the first token of an existing reasoning prefix and resuming generation substantially changes the remaining reasoning length, even though all other prefix tokens are unchanged. To trace this persistent influence, we compare next-token distributions while varying only the first token and find that sensitivity is concentrated at a small set of generation positions. Blocking attention from these positions to the first token reduces the length gap between first-token conditions. Using next-token distributions from a different first-token condition at these positions also substantially changes subsequent reasoning length. Together, these findings suggest that attention to the first token at a few sensitive positions helps sustain its length effect, illustrating how a local token choice persistently influences a sequence-level outcome.

Title: TrawMem: Reframing Agent Memory as Task-Oriented Role-Adaptive Workspaces
Authors: Mingyu Zhang, Zixu Li, Zhiheng Fu, Zhiwei Chen, Jinhe Bi, Yupeng Hu
Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents rely on memory systems to leverage long-term interactions, yet existing systems typically retrieve memories based on their relevance to the current query and use them as contextual evidence. However, relevance alone does not characterize how a memory contributes to task solving: the same memory may serve different roles across tasks, such as directly supporting the answer or linking to complementary memories with weaker semantic relevance but necessary information. We therefore reframe agent memory systems as Task-Oriented Role-Adaptive Workspaces, where memories are selected and organized by their task-oriented roles and relations. Based on this view, we propose TrawMem, which organizes interaction histories into local threads and constructs task-oriented workspaces by assigning roles and jointly selecting complementary memories. Experiments on LoCoMo and MemGallery with four open- and closed-source backbones show consistent improvements over representative memory systems, with macro-F1 gains of 2.23-3.14 points. On LoCoMo, TrawMem improves the LLM-Judge score over SimpleMem by 4.07 and 4.31 percentage points on Qwen3.5-9B and DeepSeek-V4-Flash, respectively, while requiring approximately 12.8% and 5.1% fewer context tokens, respectively.

Title: Multi-Label Agreement: A Flexible Framework for Inter-Annotator Reliability
Authors: Tim Menzner, Jochen L. Leidner
Abstract: Reliable evaluation of inter-annotator agreement (IAA) is important for assessing the consistency of annotation processes. While established IAA metrics such as Cohen's kappa, Fleiss'kappa, and Krippendorff's alpha are commonly applied in single-label settings, multi-label tasks require additional decisions about how full label sets, joint selections, and joint omissions should be compared. In this work, we present Multi-Label Agreement (MLA), a flexible framework for evaluating agreement in multi-label annotation tasks. MLA preserves the full binary label vectors assigned to each item and uses average pairwise Hamming agreement, thereby accounting for both joint selections and joint omissions. Its pooled-marginal form is not a mathematically independent coefficient: it is a chance-disagreement-weighted average of label-wise Fleiss/Scott-type coefficients and is closely related to Krippendorff's alpha with normalized Hamming distance. The framework supports pooled-marginal, Gwet AC1, and fixed-baseline normalizations, yields item-level, label-level, and corpus-level results, and includes a conditional minimum-agreement diagnostic. Through a worked example and Monte Carlo simulations, we show how the resulting values depend on label prevalence, the declared label inventory, and the selected model of expected agreement. We also provide a Python implementation. MLA thus offers a transparent and interpretable framework for multi-label agreement analysis without claiming that one normalization is universally preferable.

Title: Spatial Strategies, Not Actions: Vector-Quantized Geodesics as Tools for LLM-Driven Agents
Authors: Gabriel Turinici
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Robotics (cs.RO); Systems and Control (eess.SY)
Abstract: Large language model (LLM) based agents are often criticized for lacking spatial understanding and mainly exploiting statistical text patterns. We investigate their spatial comprehension through an architecture combining geometrical tools with a LLM serving as a high-level orchestrator in grid-world environments. The agent first collects geodesic trajectories, which are then vector-quantized to extract a representative subset. Offline, the LLM associates a natural language description of the underlying behavioral patterns to each selected trajectory, making it a tool. Online, the LLM chooses the appropriate tool conditioned on the current state and goal. Low-level control is handled by primitive actions that execute the trajectory associated with the tool. From an agentic AI perspective, this approach separates learning into two levels: tool discovery is handled through unsupervised quantization of trajectories, while reasoning and decision-making are handled by the LLM. We test the approach in a partially observable dynamic 2D grid environment with an open vision-language model (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B). Pairing the geometry-derived tool library with an agent-centered zoom tool and a collision detection tool lets a fast, non-reasoning configuration match the goal-reaching rate of a much more costly chain-of-thought version, while cutting the cost of a decision from minutes to seconds.

Title: Beyond Memory: Harnessing Long-Horizon Agents with Explicit Belief States
Authors: Yu Luo, Jiamin Jiang, Yimin Zuo, Xidao Wen, Rongchen Gao, Yongqian Sun, Shenglin Zhang, Guiyang Liu, Cheng Zhang, Fang Situ, Qi Zhou, Dan Pei
Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can now undertake increasingly complex tasks, but the way they organize interaction history into memory does not ensure a coherent understanding of the current world. We introduce PoS, an inference-time framework that constructs and continually maintains explicit belief states as the agent's decision context. Each belief combines an estimate of the current world state with unresolved task requirements, making explicit what the agent still needs to learn and accomplish. To keep this belief reliable and actionable, PoS validates its consistency and monitors task progress to detect Belief Trapping, where the agent continues to act without making meaningful progress toward the goal. Recovery is then tailored to both the trapping pattern and the type of unresolved task requirement. Experiments on four benchmarks spanning execution and diagnosis show that PoS achieves the highest overall performance on every benchmark with all three LLM backbones. Ablations demonstrate the importance of consistency validation and recovery, while context-scaling experiments show resilience to context growth. Together, these results support belief construction and continual maintenance as a foundation for long-horizon context management beyond history retention and compression.

Title: The AI Assessment Sandbox Configurator: A Framework to Support Technical Assessment in AI Regulatory Sandboxes
Authors: Alessio Buscemi, German Castignani, Daniele Pagani, Maxime Cordy, Jordi Cabot
Abstract: The EU’s Artificial Intelligence Act requires all Member States to establish AI Regulatory Sandboxes (AIRS) by August 2027: supervised environments bringing together national Competent Authorities, technical experts, and the organisations under assessment. When AIRS engagements include structured technical testing, running such testing at scale demands dedicated infrastructure, yet the tooling ecosystem remains structurally fragmented, with heterogeneous tools producing outputs that are difficult to compare, trace, and reuse. From the procedural conditions of AIRS engagements and the AI Act obligations for high-risk systems, we derive 11 architectural and governance requirements for the infrastructure that operationalises technical testing within an AIRS. In response to these requirements, we introduce the AI Assessment Sandbox Configurator, an open-source framework combining a curated Catalogue of tests and controls accessed through a stable plug-in API, a shared data model that harmonises heterogeneous outputs, role-specific dashboards for multi-disciplinary interpretation, and audiencesegmented reporting. We describe the architecture and current release, and report an early-stage pilot that exercised the harmonisation and reporting layers within a live AIRS engagement and contributed to an official Exit Report. We discuss the roadmap, the governance questions raised by the Catalogue’s tiered contribution model, and the institutional pathways through which an open-source assessment ecosystem could emerge across Member States.

Title: World Action Modeling with Progressive Visual Planning
Authors: Fei Zhang, Zhaochong An, Duncan Frost, Yikai Wang, Pengfei Liu, Ya Zhang, Michal Drozdzal, Amir Bar
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
Abstract: World action models (WAMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for robotic control by jointly predicting future visual dynamics and actions from an initial observation and instruction. However, existing WAMs struggle with long-horizon prediction, as generating dense video rollouts is highly inefficient. Some recent WAMs address this by predicting a single future frame without generating the full video, but this approach neglects how to progress toward the goal. We present ProWAM, a progressive world action model that jointly predicts actions and an ordered sequence of sparse visual sub-goals, providing explicit visual guidance to anchor action generation throughout task execution. This design scales naturally, as sub-goal prediction can be learned from large-scale action-free videos, allowing the video backbone to offload complex visual planning from the action policy. For efficient action generation, ProWAM executes a single video-backbone forward pass to cache sparse sub-goal features, eliminating iterative full-video generation and requiring only lightweight action denoising during replanning. Across extensive evaluations, ProWAM achieves superior out-of-distribution robustness. On simulation benchmarks, it sets new state-of-the-art results on LIBERO-Plus (85.8%) and randomized RoboTwin (75.7%), outperforming the strongest baseline with relative gains of up to +35.9%. On RoboCasa365, ProWAM achieves a 48.1% success rate and 18.2% on the challenging Composite-Unseen split, ranking 4th overall. Crucially, in zero-shot real-world experiments, ProWAM achieves 70.0% success, outperforming the strongest baseline by +15.0 (from 55.0% to 70.0%, a +27.3% relative gain) in novel scenes. These results demonstrate the value of progress-indexed visual foresight for closed-loop control. Our program is in https://sii-ferenas.github.io/ProWAM-page.

Title: PyINE: A Framework for Scalable Elicitation and Oversight via Code Execution
Authors: Pierre-Luc St-Charles, Alessandro Palmas, Damiano Fornasiere, Storm Lei, Mirko Bronzi, Jean-Pierre Falet, Iulian Serban, Yoshua Bengio
Abstract: Reasoning models can remain capable of solving a task while still defaulting to cheaper but misleading shortcuts. This creates a central oversight problem: when a model gives an answer with plausible but incomplete reasoning, can an overseer determine whether that output should be trusted? To study this problem, we introduce PyINE, a framework for scalable elicitation and oversight using instrumented Python programs as a verifiable execution substrate. In PyINE, programs define task environments, execution traces provide authoritative labels for outcomes and intermediate facts, and task variants can be generated mechanically rather than through static human annotation. We instantiate the framework in PyINE-v1, a first release built from nearly one million deterministic execution traces and over 500,000 matched LLM-generated code variants used for counterfactual evaluation. Using standard RL with verifiable rewards on cue-varied tasks, we train a shortcut-following model that improves substantially at predicting execution outcomes while still making systematic errors when misleading human-facing cues conflict with the program's realized behavior. We then evaluate activation probes, trained text classifiers, prompted judges, and a lightweight debate protocol as overseers of this model. We find that performance pooled at the dataset level can hide weak coverage of the failures that matter most: cheap learned overseers often miss rare shortcut-driven errors, while stronger model-based checks are more balanced but substantially costlier and harder to turn into reliable thresholded decisions. PyINE-v1 turns this failure-mode coverage problem into a reusable experimental setting for developing oversight methods that are verifiable, failure-mode-aware, and cost-sensitive.

Title: Matching Object or Relation? Tracing Abstract Reasoning Inside VLMs
Authors: Gouki Minegishi, Hiroki Furuta, Takeshi Kojima, Yusuke Iwasawa, Yutaka Matsuo
Abstract: Vision Language Models (VLMs) excel on visual benchmarks but fail systematically on tasks requiring abstract reasoning. Existing benchmarks document this failure but cannot say \emph{why} it happens or which cognitive capability is missing. We close this gap by adopting the Relational Match-to-Sample (RMTS) paradigm from comparative and developmental psychology and pairing it with a mechanistic analysis of the model's internals. On a parametrically controlled stimulus set evaluated across frontier API models (GPT, Claude, Gemini) and three open-source families (Qwen3.5, Gemma-4, InternVL3), we identify four levers that shift VLMs toward the relational match---capability tier, model scale, the number of objects per scene, and the absence of per-object stimulus noise---together producing a developmental-like trajectory that mirrors the human \emph{relational shift}. Opening up the model, a per-layer representational similarity analysis and a causal mediation analysis reveal that VLM abstract reasoning is implemented by two competing circuits: an early circuit that organises images by their surface object features, and a late circuit that organises them by their abstract relation. Extending the analysis to ARC-AGI-1, we find that ablating the relational heads identified on RMTS degrades performance more than ablating random heads, indicating that the relational circuit is recruited beyond our controlled stimuli. We hope this mechanism-level view serves as a step toward understanding how abstract reasoning is implemented in VLMs.

Title: Ream: Unfolding Mutual Awareness in Human-Agent Workspaces
Authors: Peiling Jiang, Sangho Suh, Varsha Kishore, Jonathan Bragg, Haijun Xia, Pao Siangliulue, Daniel S. Weld, Amy X. Zhang, Joseph Chee Chang
Abstract: As AI agents work alongside humans in shared workspaces, a mutual awareness challenge arises: agents act at speeds that outpace human monitoring, and users'evolving interests are not always expressed in chat. This challenge is especially pressing in literature review, where both parties retrieve, read, and synthesize a growing body of papers. We present Ream, a literature review workspace that supports mutual awareness through structured artifacts, bidirectional engagement tracking, and localized visualizations. Users can see each party's activity within these documents, and agents can retrieve the same history to guide their work. In studies with eighteen researchers, participants used these traces to inspect evidence, steer agents, communicate through annotations, and reflect on their research focus. Shared histories also helped agents build on earlier work. These findings inform how engagement traces within shared documents can support transparency, personalized assistance, and coordination in human-agent knowledge work.

Title: Learning to Accumulate Knowledge with Mutual Information
Authors: Yuyang Zhao, Lizi Liao, Leyang Shen, Xiaoyan Zhao, Yang Zhang, Fuli Feng, Xiangnan He
Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can improve their performance by reusing knowledge distilled from past interactions. However, curating new experiences into a knowledge bank that becomes more useful as it grows remains challenging. Effective knowledge accumulation should limit redundant overlap among entries and ensure that new knowledge contributes beyond what the bank already provides. Yet training a curator with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) on standalone task success can reinforce general guidance even when it duplicates existing knowledge. Therefore, we propose Knowledge Weaver, a reinforcement learning framework that trains a language model to curate reusable knowledge from agent trajectories. We couple feedback inspired by token-wise mutual information (MI) with marginal success rewards to guide knowledge accumulation. Together, these signals encourage the curator to preserve distinct information from experience and produce entries that improve task success when added to existing knowledge. Standalone success rewards also favor entries that are useful on their own. On ALFWorld and WebShop, Knowledge Weaver achieves mean success rates of 54.0\% and 42.0\% with k=10 retrieved entries, exceeding GRPO by 16.9 and 18.7 percentage points, respectively. Its knowledge banks also outperform the evaluated prompt-based and established banks, including human-written banks, in overall ALFWorld success rate and WebShop score with the executor frozen. Our codebase is available at https://github.com/LaoKuiZe/Knowledge-Weaver.

Title: Open-ended Scientific Discovery with Possibilistic Reasoning
Authors: Anita Yang, Siu Lun Chau, Tomoya Wakayama, Krikamol Muandet, Masaki Adachi
Abstract: Autonomous scientific discovery with LLMs requires generating and testing hypotheses adaptively as evidence accumulates while maintaining statistical validity. Existing anytime-valid methods can handle data-dependent hypotheses, but open-ended discovery poses a deeper challenge: the best discovered hypothesis may still be the best of a bad lot, with better explanations yet undiscovered, while even background knowledge such as physical laws may require revision in light of new findings. In response, we formalize the problem as Abductive Autonomous Scientific Discovery (AASD) using possibility theory. We introduce abductive utility, a computable measure of discovery progress, and possibility frontier search, the first algorithm for AASD, which maintains anytime validity and achieves $\varepsilon$-optimal abductive utility asymptotically under suitable conditions. Experiments on synthetic and real-world scientific-discovery tasks show strong performance.

Title: Evidence-Traceable Dynamic Interviewer Architecture for Expertise-Adaptive Qualitative Interviews Using Local LLMs
Authors: Aisvarya Adeseye, Jouni Isoaho, Adeyemi Adeseye, Seppo Virtanen, Mohammad Tahir
Abstract: Automated interviewers and conversational agents are increasingly used in research, recruitment, customer service, and education. However, many existing systems rely on fixed question sequences and provide limited context-based personalization without considering participants'knowledge, which can lead to repetitive or irrelevant follow-up questions. Therefore, there is a need for an adaptive interviewing system that can adjust question depth while maintaining conversational continuity and semantic progression. To address this, an Evidence-Traceable Dynamic Interviewer Architecture is presented using a locally hosted Large Language Model (LLM), with the interview continuously adapted throughout the entire conversation based on the participant's responses and evolving context. The interviewer profiles participants'expertise in real time to generate knowledge-appropriate questions, well-articulated responses, and smooth transition messages that support conversational continuity. A five-module prompt-driven architecture and persistent interview-state record support these functions. The interviewer was evaluated with 246 participants. Expertise Profiling module (M3) showed 78.9% exact agreement with independently reported participant expertise, with a weighted Cohen's K of 0.80. Generate Iterative Questions module (M4) showed a strong expertise-complexity association (p=.79, p<.001), and participants reported high relevance (mean 4.41), engagement (mean 4.32), and satisfaction (mean 4.38), providing evidence that the architecture's adaptive components operated consistently with their intended functions while participants reported a positive interview experience.

Title: SWEAR: Section-Wise Efficient Audio Reasoning via Self-Rated Difficulty
Authors: Yixuan Li, Minghao Lv, Xuenan Xu, Zihao Zheng, Mengyue Wu
Abstract: Recent work on large audio-language models (LALMs) explores adaptive reasoning to balance accuracy and efficiency. However, existing approaches often rely on coarse-grained difficulty estimation, overlooking the diverse factors that determine reasoning effort. We address this limitation by deriving five-dimensional difficulty scores and compressed reasoning traces from complementary offline assessments. Based on this characterization, we propose SWEAR, a difficulty-aware reasoning framework that learns difficulty signals during supervised fine-tuning and uses reinforcement learning to adapt reasoning allocation across reasoning stages. Experiments on MMAU-test-mini and MMAR show that SWEAR improves accuracy while substantially reducing generated tokens, shortening reasoning for easy instances without sacrificing performance on difficult ones.

Title: When Faster Decisions Do Not Make Better Agents: An Empirical Study of Jev in Agent Workflows
Authors: Yuchen Ling, Shengcheng Yu, Zhenyu Chen, Chunrong Fang
Abstract: AI agents depend on repeated decisions to accomplish tasks, with large language models (LLMs) commonly serving as their core decision makers. The recent emergence of Jev offers an opportunity to make these decisions faster and at lower cost. However, it remains unclear whether such local savings can be translated into efficient and reliable task completion. In this paper, we investigate this efficiency transfer across five agents in two representative application settings, embodied tasks in ALFWorld and mobile app use in AndroidWorld. Across 4,500 task executions, we jointly evaluate task effectiveness, decision-level and task-level resource use, and execution behavior. Experimental results show that Jev integration substantially reduces decision cost and latency across all five agents, with task-level gains varying by workflow. Task success remains close to baseline levels on ALFWorld and declines more substantially in two mobile agents. Auxiliary reasoning and additional interactions absorb decision savings, while failed recovery and premature completion limit successful delivery. Mean cost per successful outcome increases in one agent even as spending per attempt falls. These findings highlight the importance of preserving progress, supporting recovery, and verifying completion when integrating efficient decision models into agent workflows. Their practical value should be assessed through successful task delivery, recovery behavior, and resources per delivered outcome.

Title: Humanize Olympiad Agents: A Multi-Session Workflow for Olympiad Problem Solving with Solve, Review, Wiki, Verify
Authors: Zhengyang Zhang, Jing Xiong, Hongzhou Lin, Juihui Chung, Zijian Zhang, Song Han, Sihao Liu, Ligeng Zhu
Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are rapidly improving on long-horizon scientific and olympiad tasks. Recent systems have produced a Lean-formalized resolution of the Navier--Stokes problem and autonomous solutions to four open questions in the Erd\H{o}s Conjectures database. Yet neither system releases both its underlying model and complete inference stack. More broadly, a single agent session remains brittle on difficult problems: early errors can propagate, missing domain knowledge can stall progress, and apparent success can mask a misinterpretation or weakening of the original task. We introduce HOA (Humanize Olympiads Agent), an open, flow-level framework that coordinates multiple agent sessions through three complementary feedback channels. First, an independent reviewer evaluates each candidate and provides actionable feedback. Second, a structured wiki supplies task-specific knowledge that may be missing or unreliable in model pretraining. Third, a verifier checks generated Lean proofs against trusted challenge statements. With GPT-5.6 Sol, HOA achieves perfect scores on the IMO, IPhO, and IOI 2026, near-full marks on the IChO 2026 problem set, and solves all 672 problems (100%) on PutnamBench. On the Lean-Eval leaderboard, HOA ranks first, solving 251 of 304 problems (82.6%). We further evaluate HOA with open models. Using Kimi-K3, HOA achieves full scores on the IMO, IPhO, and IOI, and a gold-level score of 97.1% on the IChO. These results closely match the closed-source GPT-5.6 Sol + /Goal baseline on the IMO and IPhO, while exceeding it on the IChO and IOI, demonstrating that systematic feedback can help bridge substantial differences in base-model capability.

Title: VETNET: Assembling Benchmark Datasets for AI-Driven Veterinary Innovation
Authors: Katherine J. Koebel, Renata Ivanek, Parminder Basran, Jennifer Sun, Casey Cazer, Gayatri Anil, Tommaso Banzato, Liz Barton, Dottie Cimino Brown, Leszek Bukowski, Marta Castelhano, Simon Coghlan, Christopher De Sa, Nikki Dutta, Hala Ghali, Julio Giordano, Joshua Glass, David C. Hogg, Nicholas Hollingshead, Adam Kiehl, Ziang Liu, Monica Meduri, Param Mohapatra, Kim Nayyer, Amelia Nelson, Peter-John Mantyla Noble, Christopher Pinard, Beryl Rabindran, Scott Ross, Ron Seccia, Moira Sheehan, Fei Wang, Tracy L. Webb, Kilian Q. Weinberger, Heather M. Whitney, Chen Xin
Abstract: VETNET represents an ecosystem of live benchmark datasets and evaluation frameworks designed to accelerate AI-driven innovation in animal science and veterinary medicine through standardized, high-quality datasets and multi-institutional collaboration across academic and non-academic sectors. This framework addresses the gap between AI advances in human medicine and the fragmented state of veterinary AI development.

Title: Are Multimodal Benchmarks Really Useful? Item-Level Multimodal Benchmark Diagnosis via Structure-Response Co-Calibration
Authors: Shiqi Zhang, Weixin Zeng, Ziheng Zhang, Jiuyang Tang, Xiang Zhao
Abstract: Multimodal benchmarks are central to evaluating whether models can reason over information from multiple modalities. However, existing literature has revealed that some benchmarks may contain shortcut items that can be answered from a single modality or from answer-option regularities alone, thus failing to reflect models'true cross-modal inference ability. Existing methods for assessing benchmarks typically rely either on intrinsic item structure or extrinsic model response behavior, which are not adequate for a comprehensive diagnosis. To fill in this gap, we propose SRCoD, a structure-response co-calibrated diagnosis framework for item-level diagnosis of modality dependence in multimodal benchmarks.
